title: Tensor calculus
one_line_summary: Builds the differential side of tensor analysis on a manifold: why partial derivatives fail, the Lie derivative from dragging along a congruence, the affine connection and covariant derivative, parallel transport and geodesics, the Riemann tensor and flatness theorems, then the metric, its Levi-Civita connection, the curvature identities, Ricci and Einstein tensors, and the Weyl tensor with conformal structure.
role_in_book: Second of the three purely mathematical chapters (5-7) that the authors insert between special relativity and the principles of general relativity. Chapter 5 supplied tensor algebra with no derivatives and no metric; this chapter supplies every differential object the field equations need (connection, geodesic equation, Riemann, Ricci, Einstein tensor, contracted Bianchi identity) and the conformal machinery (Weyl tensor, conformal flatness) later used for gravitational radiation and Penrose diagrams. Chapter 7 then adds densities, integration, the variational derivation of the metric geodesic equation postponed here, and Killing vectors built from the Lie derivative introduced here.

learning_objectives: Reader can show from the chain rule that the partial derivative of a vector field picks up a second-derivative term under coordinate change and explain that this happens because a derivative subtracts components taken at two different points.
Reader can construct the integral curves of a vector field and use them to define and compute the Lie derivative of any tensor field, including the sign rule for upper and lower indices.
Reader can state the eight listed properties of the Lie derivative and identify the Lie derivative of a vector with the Lie bracket.

Reader can define an affine connection through the notion of a parallel vector at a neighbouring point, write the covariant derivative of vectors, covectors and general tensors, and explain why the connection transforms inhomogeneously while the covariant derivative is a tensor.
Reader can explain why the torsion and the difference of two connections are tensors, and why the sum of two connections is neither.

Reader can define the absolute derivative along a curve, parallel transport, affine geodesics, and the affine parameter, and show that reparametrization changes only the right-hand side proportional to the tangent.
Reader can compute the commutator of covariant derivatives on a vector and extract the Riemann tensor (6.40), including the torsion term for non-symmetric connections.
Reader can construct geodesic coordinates at a point with a quadratic coordinate change and say what they do and do not achieve.

Reader can reproduce the chain of results integrable connection iff Riemann tensor vanishes, symmetric plus integrable iff affine flat, hence flat iff Riemann tensor vanishes, including the infinitesimal-loop computation.
Reader can define a metric, its signature, Riemannian versus Lorentzian cases, line element, norm, angle, orthogonality, null vectors, inverse metric, and raising and lowering of indices.
Reader can write the metric geodesic equation with a general and with an interval parameter, and the null geodesic equation with an affine parameter.

Reader can derive the metric (Levi-Civita) connection by requiring affine and metric geodesics to coincide, and prove that it is the unique symmetric connection with vanishing covariant derivative of the metric.
Reader can prove that a metric is flat exactly when its Riemann tensor vanishes, using (6.77).

Reader can list the algebraic symmetries of R_abcd, count independent components n^2(n^2-1)/12, write the Bianchi identities, and build the Ricci tensor, Ricci scalar, Einstein tensor and contracted Bianchi identity.
Reader can define the Weyl tensor, state its symmetries and trace-freeness, define conformally related and conformally flat metrics, and state which quantities are conformally invariant.

teaching_approach.summary: A compact, proof-oriented components treatment close in style to the classical component texts such as Synge and Schild that it lists for further reading. Every derivative is motivated by the same obstacle stated at the outset, that a derivative subtracts tensors living at different points, and each new structure (a congruence, a connection, a metric) is introduced as the extra ingredient that makes that subtraction legitimate. Definitions are built from infinitesimal displacements and Taylor expansion, results are packaged as boxed lemmas and theorems with necessity and sufficiency proved separately, and many routine verifications are deferred to '(exercise)' or '(check)' markers keyed to the end-of-chapter list. Pictures are mostly schematic line drawings of curves and arrows on blob-shaped regions; only Figs 6.4 and 6.8 show a hatched or ribbon-like sheet in perspective, and no figure shows a concrete curved surface such as a sphere, and there is no physics in the chapter beyond the choice of Lorentzian signature.
narrative_arc: Pose the question of which differential operations are tensorial after the algebraic ones of Chapter 5.
Show by the chain rule (6.1) that partial differentiation is not, and diagnose the cause as comparison of components at two points with different transformation matrices.
Announce the plan: three derivatives, each needing an auxiliary structure (a vector field, an affine connection, a metric).

Lie derivative: vector field gives a congruence of integral curves; view a coordinate shift actively to drag a tensor along a curve; subtract at the same point; derive (6.8) for a rank-2 tensor; show it reduces to an ordinary derivative in adapted coordinates; list properties and the general formula (6.17).

Covariant derivative: posit a parallel vector at a neighbouring point with a change bilinear in the vector and the displacement; this introduces Gamma; demand tensor character to get the inhomogeneous law (6.23); extend to covectors via Leibniz and to all tensors; note torsion and restrict to symmetric connections.

Transport along curves: absolute derivative, parallel propagation as a first-order ODE, affine geodesic as a self-parallel curve, reparametrization invariance of the geodesic property, affine parameter and affine length, local existence and uniqueness versus global focusing.
Curvature appears algebraically: commutator of covariant derivatives defines R^a_bcd; tensor character follows by the quotient argument.
Tool: geodesic coordinates kill Gamma at a point but not its derivatives.

Geometric meaning of R: path dependence of parallel transport; prove integrability iff R=0 by an integrability condition (necessity) and an infinitesimal loop plus curve deformation (sufficiency); prove symmetric plus integrable iff flat with a parallel frame whose dual covectors are gradients; combine into the flatness theorem.
Add a metric: signature, lengths, angles, null cone, inverse metric, index gymnastics.
Metric geodesics as curves of stationary interval, equation quoted with Christoffel symbols (derivation postponed to Chapter 7); null geodesics.
Unify: choose Gamma equal to the Christoffel symbols so that straightest and extremal curves coincide; prove metric compatibility and its converse.
Metric flatness equals vanishing Riemann tensor for the metric connection, with (6.77) flagged for later use.
Catalogue curvature: symmetries, component count, Bianchi identities, Ricci, Ricci scalar, Einstein tensor, contracted Bianchi identity, sign-convention warning.
Close with the Weyl tensor as the trace-free part, conformal rescalings and their invariants, and two quoted theorems on conformal flatness.

sections.title: Partial derivative of a tensor
sections.summary: Having finished algebraic tensor operations, the authors ask which derivatives preserve tensor character. Differentiating the vector transformation law shows an extra term containing second derivatives of the new coordinates, so the partial derivative of a vector is not a (1,1) tensor. The deeper reason is that a derivative subtracts values at neighbouring points, where the transformation matrices differ. The remedy previewed is to add structure: a vector field (Lie derivative), an affine connection (covariant derivative) and a metric (metric connection).

sections.title: The Lie derivative
sections.summary: A congruence of curves determines a tangent vector field, and conversely a non-vanishing vector field determines integral curves by solving dx/du = X. The Lie derivative is defined by dragging a tensor from P to a nearby point Q on the integral curve through P using the infinitesimal point transformation x -> x + du X read actively, then subtracting the dragged tensor from the one already at Q and dividing by du. For a rank-2 contravariant tensor the Jacobian expansion gives L_X T^ab = X^c d_c T^ab - T^ac d_c X^b - T^cb d_c X^a. In coordinates adapted to X (X = d_1) the Lie derivative is simply d_1. The section closes with eight properties: linearity, Leibniz rule, type preservation, commuting with contraction, action on scalars (directional derivative), on vectors (Lie bracket), on covectors, and the general formula with a minus term per upper index and a plus term per lower index.

sections.title: The affine connection and covariant differentiation
sections.summary: The naive change delta X between neighbouring points is not tensorial. The authors posit a vector at Q that is 'parallel' to X at P, differing from X(P) by a small amount assumed bilinear in X and the displacement, which defines n^3 coefficients Gamma^a_bc with a conventional minus sign. The covariant derivative is the limit of the difference between X(Q) and this parallel vector, giving nabla_c X^a = d_c X^a + Gamma^a_bc X^b. Requiring this to be a (1,1) tensor forces the inhomogeneous transformation law (6.23)/(6.24), whose extra term cancels the one in (6.1). Scalars are differentiated partially, the Leibniz rule fixes the covector formula with a minus sign, and the general formula follows. Differences of connections and the torsion are tensors; the book then restricts to symmetric (torsion-free) connections and notes that partials in any Lie derivative can then be replaced by covariant derivatives.

sections.title: Affine geodesics
sections.summary: Using the notation nabla_X for contraction with X, the absolute derivative D/Du along a curve of the congruence is defined, and a tensor is parallel transported when this vanishes, a first-order ODE with a unique solution for given initial data. An affine geodesic is a curve whose tangent is transported parallel to itself up to rescaling, giving the geodesic equation with a lambda term. Only the symmetric part of Gamma enters. A change of parameter preserves the form with a new lambda (6.35), so one can always choose an affine parameter s making the right-hand side vanish; affine parameters are fixed up to s -> alpha s + beta. Affine length can compare segments of one geodesic but not of different geodesics. Locally there is a unique geodesic in each direction through a point and between nearby points, but geodesics may refocus globally.
concepts: local existence and uniqueness of geodesics

sections.title: The Riemann tensor
sections.summary: Covariant derivatives need not commute. Writing out the second covariant derivatives of a vector and subtracting, with mixed partials assumed to commute, gives a term linear in X defining R^a_bcd plus a torsion term multiplying nabla X. For symmetric connections the commutator is (1/2)R^a_bcd X^b in bracket notation, and since the left side is a tensor for arbitrary X, R is a (1,3) tensor. For symmetric connections the commutator of any tensor is expressible through R, so R = 0 is equivalent to all covariant derivatives commuting; a geometric meaning is promised for §6.7.

sections.title: Geodesic coordinates
sections.summary: At any chosen point P one can pick coordinates in which the (symmetric) connection vanishes at P. Placing P at the origin and adding a quadratic correction with constant symmetric coefficients Q, the Jacobian is the identity at P while the second derivatives equal Q, so the transformation law gives Gamma' = Gamma - Q at P; choosing Q equal to Gamma at P does it. The derivatives of Gamma generally do not vanish, the construction extends along a curve but not to a neighbourhood, and a coordinate system with Gamma zero everywhere defines affine flatness.

sections.title: Affine flatness
sections.summary: In a general affine manifold parallel transport between two points depends on the path; a connection is integrable when it does not. Lemma 1: integrable iff Riemann tensor vanishes. Necessity uses the fact that integrability gives a covariantly constant field, whose first-order PDE requires commuting mixed partials, which by the commutator identity means R X = 0 for arbitrary X. Sufficiency expands parallel transport around an infinitesimal parallelogram to second order, finding the two routes differ by -R^a_bcd X^b dx^c Dx^d, then deforms any path into any other through infinitesimal steps on a simply connected manifold. Lemma 2: symmetric and integrable iff affine flat. Sufficiency builds n parallel, linearly independent vector fields, takes the dual covector frame, uses symmetry to show those covectors are curl-free and hence gradients of n functions, and uses those functions as coordinates in which Gamma vanishes. Together: a manifold (with symmetric connection) is affine flat iff its Riemann tensor vanishes.

sections.title: The metric
sections.summary: A metric is a symmetric (0,2) tensor field with non-zero determinant. Its signature, positive minus negative eigenvalue count, is coordinate independent even though eigenvalues are not. Riemannian metrics are positive definite; relativity uses Lorentzian metrics with one positive and three negative eigenvalues (signature -2, with the +2 convention noted). The metric supplies the line element, norms, angles, orthogonality, null vectors forming a null cone in the tangent space, and an inverse metric used to raise and lower indices; index order must then be kept track of because tensors with raised and lowered indices are treated as one geometric object.

sections.title: Metric geodesics
sections.summary: For a timelike curve the interval is the integral of the square root of g(dx/du, dx/du). A timelike metric geodesic is a curve whose interval is stationary under endpoint-fixed variations (maximum, minimum or saddle). The Euler-Lagrange equations, derived in Chapter 7, are quoted in terms of Christoffel symbols of the first and second kind, with a right-hand side depending on the parametrization; choosing the parameter linear in s removes it and gives the geodesic equation plus the normalization g(dx/ds, dx/ds) = 1. Spacelike geodesics are analogous with a sign flip. Null geodesics have zero interval, admit an affine parameter defined up to linear maps, and satisfy the same equation with a null tangent.

sections.title: The metric connection
sections.summary: With both a connection and a metric a manifold has two families of 'straight' curves: affine geodesics (never change direction) and metric geodesics (extremal length), in general different (Fig. 6.11). They coincide if the connection is set equal to the Christoffel symbols of the second kind, which is automatically symmetric and transforms as a connection. From here on the book always uses this metric connection. It makes the metric covariantly constant, and conversely a symmetric connection with covariantly constant metric must be the metric connection; the Kronecker delta and inverse metric are also covariantly constant.

sections.title: Metric flatness
sections.summary: At any single point a metric can be brought to diagonal form with entries +1 or -1, and by continuity and non-singularity the signature is constant. A metric is flat if one coordinate system achieves this form everywhere. Theorem: a metric is flat iff its Riemann tensor vanishes. Necessity: constant metric means vanishing Christoffel symbols everywhere, hence vanishing derivatives and vanishing R. Sufficiency: R = 0 gives coordinates with Gamma = 0 everywhere by §6.7, and metric compatibility rewritten as (6.77) then forces the metric components to be constant, so a linear change diagonalizes them. Hence for the metric connection, metric flatness and affine flatness coincide.

sections.title: The curvature tensor
sections.summary: With the metric connection, the Riemann-Christoffel tensor depends on the metric and its first two derivatives. It is antisymmetric in its last pair, obeys a cyclic identity from symmetry of the connection, and once lowered is symmetric under exchange of pairs and antisymmetric in the first pair. These reduce the independent components from n^4 to n^2(n^2-1)/12. The differential Bianchi identities hold, most easily shown in geodesic coordinates. Contractions define the symmetric Ricci tensor and Ricci scalar, which combine into the symmetric Einstein tensor, whose divergence vanishes identically by the contracted Bianchi identities. Other sign conventions are flagged.

sections.title: The Weyl tensor
sections.summary: The curvature tensor has 0, 1, 6 and 20 independent components for n = 1, 2, 3, 4; in four dimensions ten are carried by the Ricci tensor and ten by the Weyl tensor. The Weyl (conformal) tensor is defined for n >= 4 by subtracting Ricci and scalar pieces from R_abcd; it shares Riemann's symmetries and is in addition trace-free on every pair. Conformally related metrics (g-bar = Omega^2 g) share angles, length ratios, null geodesics and the Weyl tensor with index position (1,3), which is therefore conformally invariant, unlike g, Gamma, R^a_bcd, or the Weyl tensor with other index positions. Two theorems are quoted without proof: vanishing Weyl tensor is necessary and sufficient for conformal flatness, and every two-dimensional Riemannian manifold is conformally flat.

concepts.name: non-tensorial character of the partial derivative
aliases: ordinary derivative of a tensor is not a tensor
concepts.definition: Under a change of coordinates the partial derivatives of a vector field's components acquire, besides the (1,1) tensor term, an extra term proportional to the second derivatives of the new coordinates with respect to the old, so d_b X^a is not a tensor except under linear transformations.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening question of the chapter: which differential operations are tensorial? Answered negatively by differentiating the Chapter 5 vector transformation law with the chain rule.
formulas: \partial'_c X'^a = \frac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^b}\frac{\partial x^d}{\partial x'^c}\partial_d X^b + \frac{\partial^2 x'^a}{\partial x^b\partial x^d}\frac{\partial x^d}{\partial x'^c}X^b
concepts.notes: Generalizes the Chapter 5 observation that second partial derivatives of a scalar are not tensorial.

concepts.name: comparison of tensors at different points
concepts.definition: Tensors at different points of a manifold live in different tangent spaces and transform with Jacobian matrices evaluated at those points, so their component difference has no invariant meaning; any tensorial derivative must first carry one tensor to the other's point by some added rule.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as the fundamental reason behind (6.1): the difference quotient for X^a involves transformation matrices at P and at Q.
concepts.notes: This single diagnosis is reused to motivate the Lie derivative (drag along a congruence), the connection (parallel vector) and the metric connection.

concepts.name: auxiliary structure for tensorial differentiation
concepts.definition: To differentiate tensors tensorially one must add structure to the bare manifold: a vector field gives the Lie derivative, an affine connection gives the covariant derivative, and a metric gives a preferred (metric) connection and its covariant derivative.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as a roadmap at the end of §6.1 before the three constructions are carried out.
prerequisites: comparison of tensors at different points

concepts.name: congruence of curves
concepts.definition: A family of curves filling a region of the manifold such that exactly one curve passes through each point; its tangent vectors form a vector field.
concepts.how_introduced: Starting point of §6.2: take tangent vectors dx^a/du along each curve to obtain a vector field over the manifold (Fig. 6.1).

concepts.name: integral curves of a vector field
concepts.definition: The curves x^a(u) solving dx^a/du = X^a(x(u)); through each point where X is non-zero there is locally a unique such curve, so a vector field generates a local congruence.
concepts.how_introduced: Converse of the congruence construction, explicitly likened to field lines or streamlines of vector analysis and justified by the ODE existence and uniqueness theorem (Fig. 6.2).

concepts.name: active versus passive transformation
aliases: active view of a coordinate transformation
concepts.definition: A passive transformation relabels the same point with new coordinates; an active one keeps the coordinate system and moves points, here x^a -> x^a + du X^a, so that the tensor transformation law can be reinterpreted as carrying tensors from one point to another.
concepts.how_introduced: Flagged at the start of §6.2 as the idea on which the intricate Lie derivative argument rests; the map (6.3) sends P to Q in the same chart (Fig. 6.4).
prerequisites: integral curves of a vector field
concepts.notes: Chapter 7 (§7.7) makes the active viewpoint systematic with diffeomorphisms, push-forwards and pull-backs.

concepts.name: Lie dragging
aliases: dragging a tensor along a congruence
concepts.definition: Transporting a tensor from P to a nearby point Q on the integral curve of X by applying the tensor transformation law with the Jacobian of the infinitesimal point map x -> x + du X, giving components that can be compared with the tensor field's own value at Q.
concepts.how_introduced: Pictured in Fig. 6.3 as a 'tensor' arrow at P reproduced as a dashed 'dragged-along tensor' at Q next to the actual tensor at Q; computed for T^ab in (6.5).

concepts.name: Lie derivative

concepts.name: adapted coordinates

concepts.name: parallel vector at a neighbouring point
aliases: change of a vector under parallel displacement
concepts.definition: A vector at Q = x + dx declared parallel to X(P); its components differ from X(P) by a small non-tensorial amount assumed to vanish with X or dx and to be bilinear in them, written -Gamma^a_bc X^b dx^c.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the failure of the naive difference (6.19); the difference between X(Q) and the parallel vector is required to be tensorial (6.20), drawn as a triangle of arrows in Fig. 6.5.
prerequisites: comparison of tensors at different points

concepts.name: affine connection
concepts.definition: A set of n^3 functions Gamma^a_bc on the manifold that specify parallel displacement and transform under coordinate change by the tensor law plus an inhomogeneous second-derivative term, exactly compensating the non-tensorial part of partial derivatives.
concepts.how_introduced: Emerges from the bilinear ansatz (6.21); its transformation law (6.23)/(6.24) is derived by demanding that nabla_c X^a be a (1,1) tensor.
prerequisites: parallel vector at a neighbouring point
formulas: \Gamma'^a_{bc} = \frac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^d}\frac{\partial x^e}{\partial x'^b}\frac{\partial x^f}{\partial x'^c}\Gamma^d_{ef} - \frac{\partial x^d}{\partial x'^b}\frac{\partial x^e}{\partial x'^c}\frac{\partial^2 x'^a}{\partial x^d\partial x^e}

concepts.name: inhomogeneous transformation law of the connection
concepts.definition: Because its transformation law is linear but inhomogeneous, the connection is not a tensor: it can be non-zero in one chart and zero at a point (or everywhere, if flat) in another.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off from (6.23)-(6.24) and immediately contrasted with the tensor law; later exploited in geodesic coordinates.

concepts.name: covariant derivative
concepts.definition: The tensorial derivative defined by comparing X(Q) with the vector at Q parallel to X(P), per unit coordinate displacement; for a vector it is d_c X^a + Gamma^a_bc X^b, raising the covariant rank by one.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined by a limit following Fig. 6.5 and evaluated using (6.18) and (6.21).
concepts.notes: The book stresses that the differentiation index sits last on Gamma.

concepts.name: affine manifold
concepts.definition: A manifold equipped with a continuous affine connection.
concepts.how_introduced: Named right after the connection transformation law is established.

concepts.name: covariant derivative of a covector
concepts.definition: For a covector, nabla_c X_a = d_c X_a - Gamma^b_ac X_b, obtained by requiring that the covariant derivative of a scalar be its partial derivative and that the Leibniz rule hold for X_a Y^a.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived as an exercise (Exercise 6.5) from (6.22), (6.25) and the product rule.

concepts.name: covariant derivative of a general tensor
concepts.definition: Partial derivative plus one +Gamma term for each upper index and one -Gamma term for each lower index, always with the derivative index last on Gamma.
concepts.how_introduced: Written as (6.27) and explicitly compared with the Lie derivative rule (6.17), which has the opposite sign pattern and derivatives of X instead of Gamma. Exercise 6.4 shows that covariant differentiation commutes with contraction, because nabla_c delta^a_b = 0.

concepts.name: difference of two connections is a tensor
concepts.definition: If Gamma and Gamma-hat are two connections on the same manifold, their difference transforms as a (1,2) tensor because the inhomogeneous terms cancel; their sum is neither a connection nor a tensor.
concepts.how_introduced: Noted directly from the transformation law after (6.27).
prerequisites: inhomogeneous transformation law of the connection

concepts.name: torsion tensor
concepts.definition: The antisymmetric part T^a_bc = Gamma^a_bc - Gamma^a_cb of a connection, which is a tensor because the inhomogeneous term in the law is symmetric in b and c.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced by the same cancellation argument as for differences of connections, then set to zero for the rest of the book.
prerequisites: difference of two connections is a tensor
concepts.notes: Reappears as the extra term in the commutator (6.39).

concepts.name: symmetric connection
concepts.definition: A connection with vanishing torsion, Gamma^a_bc = Gamma^a_cb; the book assumes this from §6.3 onward unless stated otherwise.
concepts.how_introduced: Imposed as a standing restriction right after torsion is defined.

concepts.name: Lie derivative written with covariant derivatives
concepts.definition: For a symmetric connection every partial derivative in a Lie derivative formula may be replaced by a covariant derivative, since the Gamma terms cancel pairwise.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted as a useful consequence of symmetry, with the vector case (6.29) left as Exercise 6.6.
concepts.notes: Shows the Lie derivative is independent of the connection and makes its tensor character manifest.

concepts.name: directional covariant derivative
concepts.definition: The covariant derivative of a tensor contracted with a vector field X, X^c nabla_c T.
concepts.how_introduced: Notation introduced at the start of §6.4 to write the absolute derivative compactly; linearity properties are Exercise 6.7.

concepts.name: absolute derivative
concepts.definition: The covariant rate of change of a tensor along a curve with tangent X = dx/du, DT/Du = X^c nabla_c T; for fields defined only on the curve it equals dT/du plus Gamma terms contracted with dx/du.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined for curves of the congruence generated by X, reusing the §6.2 link between vector fields and curves.

concepts.name: parallel transport
concepts.definition: Carrying a tensor along a curve so that its absolute derivative vanishes; as a first-order linear ODE it has a unique solution for any initial value, defining the tensor along the whole curve.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined by (6.32); its path dependence becomes the geometric meaning of curvature in §6.7 (Fig. 6.8).

concepts.name: affine geodesic
concepts.definition: A curve whose tangent vector, when parallel transported along the curve, stays proportional to the tangent; with an arbitrary parameter the tangent's absolute derivative is a multiple lambda(u) of itself.
concepts.how_introduced: Framed as the privileged curve that never changes direction; written as (6.33) and in components (6.34), with the remark that only the symmetric part of Gamma contributes.

concepts.name: reparametrization of geodesics
concepts.definition: Being an affine geodesic is a property of the image curve: under u -> u-tilde(u) the equation keeps its form with a new function lambda-tilde determined by lambda and the first two derivatives of the parameter change.
concepts.how_introduced: Explicit chain-rule computation in §6.4 ending with (6.35)-(6.36) and a '(check)'.

concepts.name: affine parameter
concepts.definition: A parameter along a geodesic for which lambda vanishes, so the tangent vector is parallel transported exactly; it is unique up to s -> alpha s + beta with constants alpha, beta. For null geodesics of a metric the same name is used for the parameter that removes the right-hand side.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by choosing u-tilde in (6.35) to kill lambda-tilde; freedom shown in Exercise 6.9; reused for null metric geodesics in §6.9.

concepts.name: affine length
concepts.definition: The integral of the affine parameter between two points of one geodesic; it can compare segments on the same geodesic but not on different geodesics because each geodesic's scale alpha is arbitrary without a metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Remark following the affine freedom s -> alpha s + beta.

concepts.name: local existence and uniqueness of geodesics
concepts.definition: Through every point in every direction there is a unique affine geodesic, and sufficiently close points are joined by a unique geodesic, both following from ODE theory; globally, geodesics from one point may meet again.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated with Figs 6.6 and 6.7 at the end of §6.4.

concepts.name: geodesic focusing
concepts.definition: Distinct geodesics leaving a point may intersect again at another point, so the uniqueness of the geodesic joining two points holds only locally.
concepts.how_introduced: One-sentence remark with Fig. 6.7 showing two geodesics from P meeting at Q.
prerequisites: local existence and uniqueness of geodesics
concepts.notes: Later relevant to gravitational lensing and to singularity theorems, not discussed here.

concepts.name: commutator of covariant derivatives
concepts.definition: The tensor nabla_c nabla_d T - nabla_d nabla_c T; for a symmetric connection it is linear in T with coefficients built from the Riemann tensor, and for a vector equals R^a_bcd X^b.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced by the observation that covariant derivatives, unlike partial derivatives, need not commute, and computed explicitly for a vector.
prerequisites: covariant derivative of a general tensor
concepts.notes: Exercise 6.10 gives the (1,1) case; Exercise 6.11 the index-free form with the Lie bracket term.

concepts.name: Riemann tensor
concepts.definition: The (1,3) tensor built from the connection and its first derivatives, R^a_bcd = d_c Gamma^a_bd - d_d Gamma^a_bc + Gamma^e_bd Gamma^a_ec - Gamma^e_bc Gamma^a_ed, measuring non-commutation of covariant derivatives and the change of a vector transported around an infinitesimal loop; it vanishes exactly when the (symmetric) connection is flat.
concepts.how_introduced: Appears algebraically from the commutator (6.39)-(6.40); tensor character by the quotient argument (6.41); geometric meaning given in §6.7; revisited with the metric connection in §6.12.

concepts.name: quotient argument for tensor character
concepts.definition: If a quantity contracted with an arbitrary tensor always yields a tensor, the quantity itself is a tensor.
concepts.how_introduced: Used to conclude that R^a_bcd is a (1,3) tensor since the left side of (6.41) is tensorial for arbitrary X.

concepts.name: geodesic coordinates
aliases: normal coordinates at a point (weak form)
concepts.definition: Coordinates about a point P in which the components of a symmetric connection vanish at P, obtained from any chart centred at P by adding a quadratic term with coefficients equal to Gamma(P); the first derivatives of Gamma are not removable in general.
concepts.how_introduced: Proved constructively in §6.6 with (6.42) and the transformation law (6.23); advertised as the easiest way to establish tensor identities.
prerequisites: inhomogeneous transformation law of the connection
concepts.notes: Used later for (6.80), (6.83), the Palatini identity (DIV ch11) and as the mathematical form of the local inertial frame of the equivalence principle (DIV ch09).

concepts.name: integrable connection
concepts.definition: A connection for which parallel transport of any vector from one point to another gives a result independent of the path, so a single vector generates a covariantly constant field over the manifold.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by Fig. 6.8: in a general affine manifold two paths give different transported vectors, so the everyday idea of parallelism fails.

concepts.name: integrability condition
concepts.definition: A first-order PDE system d_c X^a = F^a_c(x, X) can have solutions only if the second mixed partial derivatives computed from it agree, d_d d_c X^a = d_c d_d X^a.
concepts.how_introduced: Applied to the equation nabla_c X^a = 0 in the necessity half of Lemma 1.

concepts.name: parallel transport around an infinitesimal loop
concepts.definition: Transporting X along the two routes of an infinitesimal coordinate parallelogram with sides dx and Dx gives vectors differing at second order by -R^a_bcd X^b dx^c Dx^d; equivalently a vector carried round the loop changes by a Riemann term.
concepts.how_introduced: Explicit Taylor expansion to second order in the sufficiency half of Lemma 1, drawn in Fig. 6.9.

concepts.name: simply connected manifold
concepts.definition: A connected manifold in which every closed loop can be continuously shrunk to a point, equivalently any two curves with the same endpoints can be continuously deformed into each other.
concepts.how_introduced: Invoked parenthetically to pass from infinitesimal loops to finite paths (Fig. 6.10).

concepts.name: parallel frame and dual frame
concepts.definition: A set of n linearly independent vector fields X_i^a, each parallel transported, together with the inverse matrix X^i_b satisfying X^i_b X_i^a = delta^a_b; the connection can be expressed through the frame.
concepts.how_introduced: Built in the sufficiency half of Lemma 2 from integrability; symmetry of Gamma then forces the dual covectors to be curl-free and hence gradients of n scalar functions that serve as flat coordinates.

concepts.name: affine flatness
concepts.definition: A manifold with connection is affine flat if some coordinate system exists in which the connection components vanish everywhere.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined at the end of §6.6 as the global counterpart of geodesic coordinates; characterized in §6.7.

concepts.name: flatness theorem
aliases: affine flat iff Riemann tensor vanishes
Lemma: flat iff symmetric and integrable
concepts.definition: A manifold with symmetric connection is affine flat exactly when its Riemann tensor vanishes everywhere. This combines two lemmas: integrable iff R = 0, where the sufficiency half needs a simply connected manifold to pass from infinitesimal loops to finite paths; and affine flat iff symmetric and integrable.
concepts.how_introduced: Assembled from two boxed lemmas with necessity and sufficiency proofs; necessity of Lemma 2 is Exercise 6.12.

concepts.name: metric tensor
concepts.definition: A symmetric (0,2) tensor field g_ab with non-vanishing determinant at every point, used to assign squared lengths, angles and a causal classification to vectors and to identify vectors with covectors.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced abruptly as the third auxiliary structure promised in §6.1, via its determinant and eigenvalues.

concepts.name: signature
concepts.definition: The number of positive minus the number of negative eigenvalues of the matrix g_ab at a point (equivalently of +1 minus -1 entries in a diagonalized form); there are no zero eigenvalues since the determinant is non-zero, and the signature is independent of coordinates and constant on a connected manifold for a continuous non-degenerate metric.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in §6.8 with two unanswered 'why?' prompts; invariance argued in §6.11 from pointwise diagonalization and continuity.
concepts.notes: The invariance under coordinate change is Sylvester's law of inertia, which the book does not name.

concepts.name: Riemannian metric
concepts.definition: A metric all of whose eigenvalues are positive, so that every non-zero vector has positive squared length; a manifold carrying one is a Riemannian manifold.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as the case in which the metric defines genuine distances and lengths.

concepts.name: Lorentzian metric
concepts.definition: A metric with one positive and (in four dimensions) three negative eigenvalues, so signature -2 in the book's convention; other authors use the opposite overall sign with signature +2.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as the case relevant to relativity, with the alternative convention flagged in parentheses.

concepts.name: line element
concepts.definition: The quadratic expression ds^2 = g_ab dx^a dx^b giving the squared infinitesimal distance (or interval) between neighbouring points; ds^2 means the square of ds.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined immediately after Riemannian metrics; used in the exercises to read off g_ab from line elements of flat 3-space and Minkowski space.

concepts.name: norm of a vector
concepts.definition: The scalar X^2 = g_ab X^a X^b; for a Lorentzian metric it can be positive, negative or zero.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined together with positive definiteness.

concepts.name: null vector and null cone
aliases: light cone in the tangent space
concepts.definition: A non-zero vector with zero norm is null; the null vectors at P form a cone in the tangent space T_P M that separates timelike from spacelike vectors, exactly as in special relativity.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained from the indefiniteness of a Lorentzian metric and linked back to the special relativistic null cone.

concepts.name: angle between vectors
concepts.definition: For non-null X and Y, cos(X,Y) = g_ab X^a Y^b divided by the square roots of the absolute values of their norms.
concepts.how_introduced: Given as a further use of the metric; needed later to show angles are conformally invariant.

concepts.name: orthogonality
concepts.definition: Vectors are orthogonal when g_ab X^a Y^b = 0; in particular a null vector is orthogonal to itself.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated after the angle formula with the self-orthogonality remark.

concepts.name: inverse metric
concepts.definition: The matrix inverse g^ab of g_ab, defined by g_ab g^bc = delta_a^c; it is a symmetric (2,0) tensor.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in components with the remark that tensor character is not obvious; Exercise 6.13 proves it.

concepts.name: raising and lowering indices
concepts.definition: Contracting with g_ab lowers an index and with g^ab raises one; tensors related this way are treated as different component representations of one geometric object and share a kernel letter.
concepts.how_introduced: Introduced with (6.58)-(6.59) once the inverse metric exists.

concepts.name: order of mixed indices
concepts.definition: When indices can be raised and lowered, their left-to-right order matters: X_a^b (first slot lowered) and X^b_a (second slot lowered) are in general different arrays.
concepts.how_introduced: Warning at the end of §6.8.

concepts.name: interval along a curve
concepts.definition: For a timelike curve x^a(u), the integral from P1 to P2 of the square root of g_ab (dx^a/du)(dx^b/du) du, independent of the parametrization.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by dividing the line element by du^2 in §6.9.

concepts.name: metric geodesic
concepts.definition: A curve between two points whose interval is stationary under small variations fixed at the endpoints; the stationary value may be a maximum, minimum or saddle.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined variationally, with the Euler-Lagrange derivation postponed to Chapter 7 and the resulting equations quoted.

concepts.name: Christoffel symbols of the first kind
concepts.definition: The combinations {ab,c} = (1/2)(d_b g_ac + d_a g_bc - d_c g_ab) of first derivatives of the metric; symmetric in a and b and not a tensor.
concepts.how_introduced: Appear in the quoted Euler-Lagrange form of the metric geodesic equation.

concepts.name: Christoffel symbols of the second kind
concepts.definition: The first-kind symbols with the index raised, {a bc} = g^ad {bc,d}.
concepts.how_introduced: Produced by multiplying the geodesic equation by g^ad; then identified with the metric connection in §6.10.
prerequisites: Christoffel symbols of the first kind

concepts.name: proper parametrization of metric geodesics
concepts.definition: If the parameter u is a linear function of the interval s, the right-hand side of the metric geodesic equation vanishes; with u = s the tangent has unit norm.
concepts.how_introduced: Read off from the factor (d^2s/du^2)/(ds/du) in (6.64).

concepts.name: spacelike geodesic
concepts.definition: The analogue of a timelike metric geodesic for curves with spacelike tangent, using the proper distance d sigma^2 = -g_ab dx^a dx^b.
concepts.how_introduced: One-sentence remark after (6.68).

concepts.name: null geodesic
concepts.definition: A geodesic of an indefinite metric along which the interval between any two points is zero, i.e. with null tangent; with an affine parameter it satisfies the geodesic equation with no right-hand side, the parameter being fixed up to linear maps.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated after timelike and spacelike geodesics, with the parametrization claim asserted rather than derived.
concepts.notes: Conformally related metrics share null geodesics (§6.13, Exercise 6.29).

concepts.name: affine versus metric geodesics
concepts.definition: On a manifold with independent connection and metric there are two families of privileged curves: affine geodesics, which never change direction, and metric geodesics, which extremize length; in Euclidean space both are straight lines, but in general they differ.
concepts.how_introduced: Opening of §6.10 with Fig. 6.11 showing two differently oriented hatchings of curves on a manifold.

concepts.name: metric connection
concepts.definition: The unique symmetric connection built from the metric, Gamma^a_bc = (1/2) g^ad (d_b g_dc + d_c g_db - d_d g_bc), for which affine and metric geodesics coincide; the book uses only this connection from §6.10 on.
concepts.how_introduced: Obtained by comparing the affine geodesic equation (6.37) with the metric one (6.67) and demanding they agree; symmetric by inspection, connection-like transformation left to Exercise 6.17.
prerequisites: Christoffel symbols of the second kind

concepts.name: metric compatibility
concepts.definition: With the metric connection the covariant derivative of the metric vanishes identically, and so does that of the inverse metric. Raising and lowering indices therefore commutes with covariant differentiation. The Kronecker delta is covariantly constant for any connection (Exercise 6.4); the book simply lists it alongside.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as an identity with proof left to Exercise 6.20, which also deduces nabla_b X_a = g_ac nabla_b X^c.
prerequisites: covariant derivative of a general tensor

concepts.name: fundamental theorem for the metric connection
concepts.definition: For a symmetric connection, the covariant derivative of the metric vanishes if and only if the connection is the metric connection.
concepts.how_introduced: Boxed theorem in §6.10; the converse is Exercise 6.21, solved by permuting indices in (6.77) and adding.

concepts.name: derivative of the metric in terms of the connection
concepts.definition: Metric compatibility rearranged: d_c g_ab = Gamma^d_ac g_db + Gamma^d_bc g_ad, so the first derivatives of the metric vanish wherever the connection components do.
concepts.how_introduced: Derived inside the metric flatness proof and explicitly flagged as useful later.
concepts.notes: Used in DIV ch07 to derive the contracted Christoffel identity and in Exercise 6.21.

concepts.name: flat metric
concepts.definition: A metric for which some coordinate system makes g_ab diagonal with every diagonal entry +1 or -1 at every point (not just at one point).
concepts.how_introduced: Contrasted in §6.11 with the always-available pointwise diagonalization.

concepts.name: metric flatness theorem
aliases: flat iff Riemann tensor vanishes (metric version)
concepts.definition: A metric is flat if and only if the Riemann tensor of its metric connection vanishes; hence for the metric connection metric flatness and affine flatness coincide.
concepts.how_introduced: Boxed theorem in §6.11 proved with the §6.7 theorem and (6.77).
prerequisites: derivative of the metric in terms of the connection

concepts.name: algebraic symmetries of the Riemann tensor
concepts.definition: With the metric connection, R_abcd is antisymmetric in its last pair and in its first pair, symmetric under exchange of the two pairs, and satisfies the cyclic identity on its last three indices.
concepts.how_introduced: (6.78) is immediate from the definition, (6.79) from symmetry of Gamma, (6.80) via geodesic coordinates, (6.81) by combination.

concepts.name: cyclic identity
concepts.definition: For a symmetric connection the sum of R^a_bcd over cyclic permutations of b, c, d vanishes, equivalently R^a_[bcd] = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Listed as (6.79) with proof in Exercise 6.24.

concepts.name: number of independent Riemann components
concepts.definition: The symmetries reduce the n^4 components of R_abcd to n^2(n^2 - 1)/12 independent ones: 0, 1, 6 and 20 for n = 1, 2, 3, 4.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated after the symmetry summary (6.82) and tabulated case by case at the start of §6.13.
prerequisites: algebraic symmetries of the Riemann tensor

concepts.name: Bianchi identities
concepts.definition: The cyclic sum over three indices of the covariant derivative of R_de.. vanishes: nabla_a R_debc + nabla_c R_deab + nabla_b R_deca = 0, equivalently R_de[ab;c] = 0.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted as most easily proved in geodesic coordinates; proof in Exercise 6.25.

concepts.name: Ricci tensor
concepts.definition: The contraction of the Riemann tensor on its first and third indices, R_ab = R^c_acb, symmetric by pair symmetry.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in §6.12 as the first of several tensors built from curvature.

concepts.name: Ricci scalar
concepts.definition: The trace of the Ricci tensor, R = g^ab R_ab.
concepts.how_introduced: Final contraction after the Ricci tensor.

concepts.name: Einstein tensor
concepts.definition: The symmetric tensor G_ab = R_ab - (1/2) g_ab R, whose covariant divergence vanishes identically.
concepts.how_introduced: Built from Ricci tensor and scalar in §6.12 without physical motivation; it becomes the left side of the field equations in DIV ch10.

concepts.name: contracted Bianchi identities
concepts.definition: Contracting the Bianchi identities twice gives nabla_b G_a^b = 0 identically.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as a consequence of (6.83); deduced in Exercise 6.25.
concepts.notes: Key later for compatibility of the field equations with conservation of energy-momentum.

concepts.name: curvature sign conventions
concepts.definition: Authors differ in the overall sign of the Riemann tensor, the choice of contraction for the Ricci tensor, and the metric signature, so formulas must be checked against a book's conventions.
concepts.how_introduced: Closing remark of §6.12, echoing the signature remark of §6.8.

concepts.name: Weyl tensor
concepts.definition: For n >= 4, the part of the Riemann tensor left after subtracting terms built from the Ricci tensor, Ricci scalar and metric so that every contraction vanishes; in four dimensions it carries the 10 curvature components not fixed by R_ab.
concepts.how_introduced: Motivated by the component count in n = 4 (20 = 10 Ricci + 10 Weyl) and defined by an explicit formula (6.88).
formulas: C_{abcd} = R_{abcd} + \tfrac12(g_{ad}R_{cb} + g_{bc}R_{da} - g_{ac}R_{db} - g_{bd}R_{ca}) + \tfrac16(g_{ac}g_{db} - g_{ad}g_{cb})R

concepts.name: trace-free property of the Weyl tensor
concepts.definition: The Weyl tensor has all the algebraic symmetries of R_abcd and in addition C^a_bad = 0, which together imply that every contraction of any pair of its indices vanishes.
concepts.how_introduced: Stated as (6.89)-(6.90), proof in Exercise 6.27.
prerequisites: algebraic symmetries of the Riemann tensor

concepts.name: conformally related metrics
concepts.definition: Two metrics on the same manifold with g-bar_ab = Omega^2 g_ab for a non-vanishing differentiable function Omega; they agree on angles, ratios of lengths and null directions but not on lengths.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined in §6.13; invariance of angles and ratios follows from (6.53) and (6.55) (Exercise 6.28).

concepts.name: conformal invariance
concepts.definition: A quantity is conformally invariant if it is unchanged when the metric is replaced by a conformally related one; examples are angles, null geodesics and the Weyl tensor C^a_bcd with one index up, while g_ab, Gamma, R^a_bcd and the Weyl tensor in other index positions are not.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined via (6.92) with an explicit warning about index position.
concepts.notes: Exercise 6.29 (null geodesics) and 6.30 (transformation of Gamma and Riemann) supply the proofs.

concepts.name: conformally flat metric
concepts.definition: A metric expressible as Omega^2 times a flat metric in some coordinate system.
concepts.how_introduced: Defined at the end of §6.13 before two quoted theorems.

concepts.name: Weyl criterion for conformal flatness
concepts.definition: A metric is conformally flat if and only if its Weyl tensor vanishes everywhere. The book's box gives no dimension restriction. The statement is correct for n >= 4, which is also the range where the book defines C_abcd; in n = 3 the Weyl tensor vanishes identically and the Cotton tensor decides instead.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted without proof as the first closing theorem of §6.13.
concepts.notes: The book does not restate the n >= 4 restriction in the theorem box; in three dimensions the Weyl tensor vanishes identically and a different (Cotton) tensor decides conformal flatness.

concepts.name: conformal flatness in two dimensions
concepts.definition: Every two-dimensional Riemannian metric is (locally) conformally flat; Exercise 6.31 proves the Lorentzian analogue using null coordinates.
concepts.how_introduced: Quoted without proof as the second closing theorem of §6.13.
concepts.notes: Used in DIV ch18 to build Penrose diagrams of two-dimensional sections.

concepts.name: tangent space
concepts.definition: The vector space of tangent vectors at a point P of a manifold; tensors at P live in products of it and its dual.
concepts.how_introduced: Relied on from Chapter 5; named explicitly when the null cone is placed in T_P M.

key_equations.name: Transformation of the partial derivative of a vector
key_equations.latex: \partial'_c X'^a = \frac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^b}\frac{\partial x^d}{\partial x'^c}\partial_d X^b + \frac{\partial^2 x'^a}{\partial x^b\partial x^d}\frac{\partial x^d}{\partial x'^c}X^b
key_equations.meaning: The first term is the (1,1) tensor law; the second, involving second derivatives of the coordinate change, spoils tensor character unless the transformation is linear.
key_equations.symbols: X^a vector components; x^a old, x'^a new coordinates

key_equations.name: Components at two points use different Jacobians
key_equations.latex: X'^a_P = \left[\frac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^b}\right]_P X^b_P, \qquad X'^a_Q = \left[\frac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^b}\right]_Q X^b_Q
key_equations.meaning: Why a difference quotient of components is not tensorial: the transformation matrices are evaluated at different points.

key_equations.name: Integral curves
key_equations.meaning: ODE whose solutions are the curves of the congruence generated by a vector field.

key_equations.name: Infinitesimal point transformation
key_equations.meaning: Actively maps P to a nearby point Q on the integral curve through P, in the same chart.
Jacobian of the point map, identity plus a first-order correction.

key_equations.name: Dragged-along tensor
key_equations.latex: \tilde{T}^{ab}(\tilde{x}) = \frac{\partial\tilde{x}^a}{\partial x^c}\frac{\partial\tilde{x}^b}{\partial x^d}T^{cd}(x) = T^{ab}(x) + [\partial_c X^a T^{cb}(x) + \partial_d X^b T^{ad}(x)]\delta u + O(\delta u^2)
key_equations.meaning: Components at Q of the tensor carried from P by the point map.

key_equations.name: Tensor already at Q
key_equations.meaning: First-order Taylor expansion of the field at the displaced point.

key_equations.name: Definition of the Lie derivative
key_equations.meaning: Compare the field's own value at Q with the value dragged from P.

key_equations.name: Lie derivative of a (2,0) tensor
key_equations.latex: \mathrm{L}_X T^{ab} = X^c\partial_c T^{ab} - T^{ac}\partial_c X^b - T^{cb}\partial_c X^a
key_equations.meaning: Directional derivative minus one correction per upper index from the flow's shear.

key_equations.name: Adapted coordinates
key_equations.meaning: In coordinates whose x^1 lines are the integral curves, Lie differentiation is plain partial differentiation.
key_equations.symbols: starred equals: holds only in special coordinates

key_equations.name: Linearity
key_equations.meaning: Linear over constants.

key_equations.name: Leibniz rule
key_equations.meaning: Product rule for tensor products.

key_equations.name: Commutes with contraction
key_equations.meaning: Contracting before or after Lie differentiation gives the same result (proved via L_X delta = 0 in Exercise 6.1).
key_equations.symbols: Printed as delta^b_a L_X T^a_b = L_X T^a_a (checked on the rendered page); the reading copy misplaces the delta indices.

key_equations.name: Lie derivative of a scalar
key_equations.meaning: Directional derivative along X.

key_equations.name: Lie derivative of a vector
key_equations.meaning: Equals the Lie bracket.

key_equations.name: Lie derivative of a covector
key_equations.meaning: Lower indices get a plus-sign correction.

key_equations.name: General Lie derivative
key_equations.latex: \mathrm{L}_X T^{a\cdots}_{b\cdots} = X^c\partial_c T^{a\cdots}_{b\cdots} - T^{c\cdots}_{b\cdots}\partial_c X^a - \cdots + T^{a\cdots}_{c\cdots}\partial_b X^c + \cdots
key_equations.meaning: Rule for any tensor: minus per upper index, plus per lower index.

key_equations.name: Naive change of a vector
key_equations.latex: X^a(x+\delta x) = X^a(x) + \delta x^b\partial_b X^a, \qquad \delta X^a = \delta x^b\partial_b X^a
key_equations.meaning: First-order change of the field, non-tensorial.

key_equations.name: Tensorial difference vector
key_equations.meaning: Difference at Q between the actual field and the parallel vector, required to be tensorial.
key_equations.symbols: bar-delta X change under parallel displacement

key_equations.name: Parallel displacement ansatz
key_equations.meaning: Change of components under parallel displacement is bilinear in the vector and the displacement; the minus sign is conventional.

key_equations.name: Covariant derivative as a limit
key_equations.meaning: Difference between X at Q and the vector at Q parallel to X at P per unit displacement.

key_equations.name: Covariant derivative of a vector
key_equations.meaning: Tensorial derivative; the derivative index is the last lower index of Gamma.

key_equations.name: Transformation law of the connection
key_equations.latex: \Gamma'^a_{bc} = \frac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^d}\frac{\partial x^e}{\partial x'^b}\frac{\partial x^f}{\partial x'^c}\Gamma^d_{ef} - \frac{\partial x^d}{\partial x'^b}\frac{\partial x^e}{\partial x'^c}\frac{\partial^2 x'^a}{\partial x^d\partial x^e}
key_equations.meaning: Tensor law plus an inhomogeneous term that cancels the one in (6.1); defines what a connection is.

key_equations.name: Alternative connection law
key_equations.latex: \Gamma'^a_{bc} = \frac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^d}\frac{\partial x^e}{\partial x'^b}\frac{\partial x^f}{\partial x'^c}\Gamma^d_{ef} + \frac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^d}\frac{\partial^2 x^d}{\partial x'^b\partial x'^c}
key_equations.meaning: Equivalent form obtained by differentiating the identity Jacobian times inverse Jacobian equals delta (Exercise 6.3).
Covariant derivative of a scalar is its gradient.

key_equations.name: Covariant derivative of a covector
key_equations.meaning: Forced by the Leibniz rule; minus sign for lower indices.

key_equations.name: Covariant derivative of a general tensor
key_equations.meaning: One Gamma term per index, plus for upper and minus for lower.

key_equations.name: Torsion tensor
key_equations.meaning: Antisymmetric part of the connection, a tensor.

key_equations.name: Symmetric connection
key_equations.meaning: Vanishing torsion; assumed from here on.

key_equations.name: Lie derivative with covariant derivatives
key_equations.latex: \mathrm{L}_X Y^a = X^b\partial_b Y^a - Y^b\partial_b X^a = X^b\nabla_b Y^a - Y^b\nabla_b X^a
key_equations.meaning: For a symmetric connection partials may be swapped for covariant derivatives.
Directional covariant derivative.

key_equations.name: Absolute derivative
key_equations.meaning: Covariant rate of change along a curve with tangent X.

key_equations.name: Parallel transport
key_equations.meaning: First-order ODE defining a parallel tensor along a curve.

key_equations.name: Affine geodesic (general parameter)
key_equations.meaning: Tangent stays parallel to itself up to rescaling.

key_equations.name: Affine geodesic in components
key_equations.meaning: Only the symmetric part of Gamma contributes.

key_equations.name: Reparametrization chain rule
key_equations.meaning: Changing parameter only changes the coefficient of the tangent on the right.

key_equations.name: New geodesic function
key_equations.meaning: Form invariance of the geodesic equation; choosing u-tilde to make lambda-tilde zero gives an affine parameter.

key_equations.name: Affinely parametrized geodesic equation
key_equations.meaning: Tangent vector is exactly parallel transported.

key_equations.name: Affine freedom
key_equations.meaning: Only affine reparametrizations preserve affineness (Exercise 6.9).

key_equations.name: Second covariant derivative of a vector
key_equations.meaning: Treating nabla_c X^a as a (1,1) tensor and differentiating again. The reading copy garbles the last bracket; the rendered page confirms the index e on the partial derivative.

key_equations.name: Commutator of covariant derivatives
key_equations.meaning: Curvature term plus a torsion term.

key_equations.name: Riemann tensor
key_equations.meaning: Curvature from the connection and its first derivatives; same index convention as Misner-Thorne-Wheeler.

key_equations.name: Commutator for a symmetric connection
key_equations.meaning: Tensor character of R by the quotient argument.

key_equations.name: Quadratic coordinate change
key_equations.meaning: Construction of geodesic coordinates about P at the origin.

key_equations.name: Jacobian and Hessian of the change
key_equations.latex: \frac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^d} = \delta^a_d + Q^a_{bd}x^b, \qquad \frac{\partial^2 x'^a}{\partial x^d\partial x^e} = Q^a_{de}
key_equations.meaning: Jacobian equals the identity at P. The printed page shows x^d where x^b is required (d would appear three times).

key_equations.name: Geodesic coordinates
key_equations.meaning: Connection can be removed at one point; its derivatives in general cannot.

key_equations.name: Covariantly constant field
key_equations.meaning: Consequence of path-independent transport, since the curve direction is arbitrary.

key_equations.name: Integrability condition
key_equations.meaning: Mixed partials must commute for (6.44) to have solutions.

key_equations.name: Commutator with partial derivatives kept
key_equations.meaning: Form of (6.39) used in the necessity proof, so R X = 0 iff mixed partials commute.

key_equations.name: Transport along one route of an infinitesimal loop
key_equations.latex: X^a(x+\delta x+\Delta x) = X^a - \Gamma^a_{bc}X^b\delta x^c - \Gamma^a_{bc}X^b\Delta x^c - \partial_d\Gamma^a_{bc}X^b\delta x^d\Delta x^c + \Gamma^a_{bc}\Gamma^b_{ef}X^e\delta x^f\Delta x^c
key_equations.meaning: Second-order Taylor expansion of two successive parallel displacements, first along delta x then along Delta x.

key_equations.name: Loop discrepancy
key_equations.latex: \Delta X^a = (\partial_d\Gamma^a_{bc} - \partial_c\Gamma^a_{bd} + \Gamma^a_{ed}\Gamma^e_{bc} - \Gamma^a_{ec}\Gamma^e_{bd})X^b\delta x^c\Delta x^d = R^a_{bdc}X^b\delta x^c\Delta x^d = -R^a_{bcd}X^b\delta x^c\Delta x^d
key_equations.meaning: The two routes differ by a Riemann term proportional to the loop area element; zero for all loops iff R = 0. The reading copy garbles the last Gamma product; the rendered page gives Gamma^a_ec Gamma^e_bd.

key_equations.name: Dual frame
key_equations.meaning: Inverse of the matrix of n parallel vector fields, summed over bold i.
key_equations.symbols: bold i labels the frame vectors

key_equations.name: Connection from a parallel frame
key_equations.meaning: Obtained by multiplying the propagation equation for each frame vector by the dual frame. OCR garbles this; confirmed from the rendered page.

key_equations.latex: X_i^{\ a}\partial_c X^i_{\ b} = -X^i_{\ b}\partial_c X_i^{\ a} = \Gamma^a_{bc}
key_equations.meaning: Differentiating (6.46) and using (6.47).

key_equations.name: Dual covectors are curl-free
key_equations.latex: X_i^{\ a}(\partial_c X^i_{\ b} - \partial_b X^i_{\ c}) = \Gamma^a_{bc} - \Gamma^a_{cb} = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; X^i_{\ b} = \partial_b f^i
key_equations.meaning: Symmetry of the connection makes each dual covector locally a gradient.

key_equations.name: Flat coordinates from the frame
key_equations.latex: x'^a = f^a(x), \quad \frac{\partial x'^a}{\partial x^b} = X^a_{\ b}, \quad \frac{\partial x^a}{\partial x'^b} = X_b^{\ a}
key_equations.meaning: Jacobians of the new coordinates are the dual frame and the frame.

key_equations.name: Connection vanishes in the new coordinates
key_equations.latex: X_a^{\ h}\Gamma'^a_{bc} = X_a^{\ h}(X^a_{\ d}X_b^{\ e}X_c^{\ f}\Gamma^d_{ef} - X_b^{\ e}X_c^{\ f}\partial_e X^a_{\ f}) = \delta^h_d X_b^{\ e}X_c^{\ f}\Gamma^d_{ef} - X_b^{\ e}X_c^{\ f}\Gamma^h_{ef} \equiv 0
key_equations.meaning: Completes sufficiency in Lemma 2. Bold (frame) indices are lost in the reading copy; transcription follows the rendered page.

key_equations.name: Metric determinant
key_equations.meaning: Non-singularity condition defining a metric.

key_equations.name: Line element
key_equations.meaning: Squared infinitesimal distance or interval.

key_equations.name: Norm of a vector
key_equations.meaning: Squared length; sign indicates causal type for a Lorentzian metric.

key_equations.name: Null vector
key_equations.meaning: Non-zero vectors of zero norm, forming the null cone in T_P M.

key_equations.name: Angle between vectors
key_equations.meaning: Defined for non-null vectors.

key_equations.name: Orthogonality
key_equations.meaning: A null vector is orthogonal to itself.

key_equations.name: Inverse metric
key_equations.meaning: Defines the contravariant metric, a (2,0) tensor (Exercise 6.13).

key_equations.name: Lowering and raising
key_equations.latex: T_{\cdots a\cdots} = g_{ab}T^{\cdots b\cdots}, \qquad T^{\cdots a\cdots} = g^{ab}T_{\cdots b\cdots}
key_equations.meaning: Same kernel letter for all index positions.
Squared rate of interval along a parametrized curve.

key_equations.name: Interval along a curve
key_equations.meaning: Functional whose stationary curves are timelike metric geodesics.

key_equations.name: Metric geodesic equation, first-kind form
key_equations.meaning: Euler-Lagrange equations of (6.61) with general parameter, quoted ahead of Chapter 7.

key_equations.name: Christoffel symbols of the first kind
key_equations.meaning: First derivatives of the metric.

key_equations.name: Metric geodesic equation, second-kind form
key_equations.meaning: Same structure as the affine geodesic equation (6.34).

key_equations.name: Christoffel symbols of the second kind
key_equations.meaning: Raise the last index of the first-kind symbol.
Parameters linear in the interval remove the right-hand side.

key_equations.name: Metric geodesic parametrized by interval
key_equations.meaning: Timelike geodesic with unit tangent.

key_equations.name: Spacelike proper distance
key_equations.meaning: Used for spacelike geodesics with signature -2.

key_equations.name: Null geodesics
key_equations.meaning: Affinely parametrized null geodesic; u fixed up to u -> alpha u + beta.

key_equations.name: Condition for geodesics to coincide
key_equations.meaning: Choice of connection that makes straightest and extremal curves agree.

key_equations.name: Metric connection
key_equations.meaning: The Levi-Civita connection, used exclusively from here on.
Metric connection is automatically symmetric.

key_equations.name: Metric compatibility
key_equations.meaning: Metric is covariantly constant; for symmetric connections this characterizes the metric connection.
Kronecker delta and inverse metric are also covariantly constant.

key_equations.name: Metric compatibility written out
key_equations.meaning: Starting point for (6.77).

key_equations.name: Metric derivatives from the connection
key_equations.meaning: Shows metric components are constant where Gamma vanishes identically; flagged for later use.
Antisymmetry in the last pair, immediate from (6.40).

key_equations.name: Cyclic identity
key_equations.meaning: Follows from symmetry of the connection; equivalent to R^a_[bcd] = 0.

key_equations.name: Pair symmetry
key_equations.meaning: Proved in geodesic coordinates (Exercise 6.24).
Antisymmetry in the first pair.

key_equations.name: Riemann symmetries
key_equations.meaning: Complete list of algebraic symmetries of the lowered tensor.

key_equations.name: Independent components
key_equations.meaning: Riemann components in n dimensions: 1, 6, 20 for n = 2, 3, 4.

key_equations.name: Bianchi identities
key_equations.meaning: Differential identity, equivalent to R_de[ab;c] = 0.

key_equations.name: Ricci tensor
key_equations.meaning: Contraction on first and third indices; symmetric.

key_equations.name: Ricci scalar
key_equations.meaning: Curvature scalar.

key_equations.name: Einstein tensor
key_equations.meaning: Symmetric, divergence-free curvature tensor.

key_equations.name: Contracted Bianchi identities
key_equations.meaning: Identically conserved; later matched to conservation of energy-momentum.

key_equations.name: Weyl tensor in n dimensions
key_equations.latex: C_{abcd} = R_{abcd} + \frac{1}{n-2}(g_{ad}R_{cb} + g_{bc}R_{da} - g_{ac}R_{db} - g_{bd}R_{ca}) + \frac{1}{(n-1)(n-2)}(g_{ac}g_{db} - g_{ad}g_{cb})R
key_equations.meaning: Riemann minus its Ricci and scalar parts, for n >= 4.

key_equations.name: Weyl tensor in four dimensions
key_equations.latex: C_{abcd} = R_{abcd} + \tfrac12(g_{ad}R_{cb} + g_{bc}R_{da} - g_{ac}R_{db} - g_{bd}R_{ca}) + \tfrac16(g_{ac}g_{db} - g_{ad}g_{cb})R
key_equations.meaning: Trace-free part of curvature in spacetime.

key_equations.name: Weyl symmetries
key_equations.meaning: Same algebraic symmetries as Riemann.

key_equations.name: Trace-free condition
key_equations.meaning: Together with (6.89), every contraction vanishes.

key_equations.name: Conformal relation
key_equations.meaning: Pointwise rescaling of the metric by a non-zero function.

key_equations.name: Conformal invariance of Weyl
key_equations.meaning: Holds only with one index up and three down.

key_equations.name: Conformally flat metric
key_equations.meaning: Conformal to a flat metric; for n >= 4 equivalent to vanishing Weyl tensor.

key_equations.name: Conformal change of the connection (Exercise 6.30(ii))
key_equations.meaning: How the metric connection shifts under a conformal rescaling; basis for the invariance of null geodesics and of the Weyl tensor.

key_equations.name: Two-dimensional Lorentzian metric in null coordinates (Exercise 6.31)
key_equations.meaning: Null coordinates exhibit a 2D Lorentzian metric as conformally flat.

figures.label: Fig. 6.1
figures.caption_paraphrase: A family of curves filling a region yields a field of tangent vectors.
figures.visual_description: Two rounded blob-shaped regions side by side. The left blob is filled with about six gently curving, roughly parallel curves, each carrying small arrowheads. The right blob shows the same curves replaced by many short arrows tangent to where the curves were, scattered over the region.
figures.what_it_teaches: Going from a congruence of curves to its tangent vector field.
concepts: integral curves of a vector field

redesign.idea: Two-way flow explorer: the learner either sketches curves and sees tangent arrows appear, or edits a vector field formula and sees integral curves grow from seed points.
redesign.interaction: Toggle curves-to-field and field-to-curves modes; click to seed integral curves; slider for arrow density; preset fields (rotation, shear, saddle).

figures.label: Fig. 6.2
figures.caption_paraphrase: A vector field determines locally a congruence of curves.
figures.visual_description: Two blob-shaped regions. The left is filled with short arrows forming a vector field; the right shows the same arrows threaded into curving integral curves, the arrows lying along them.
figures.what_it_teaches: The converse construction: solving dx/du = X gives integral curves, like field lines.
concepts: integral curves of a vector field

redesign.idea: Merge with Fig. 6.1 into a single flow explorer; show a numerical ODE integrator tracing a curve step by step from a clicked point.
redesign.interaction: Click a point to launch an integral curve; step size slider shows Euler steps converging to the smooth curve.

figures.label: Fig. 6.3
figures.caption_paraphrase: Tensors at neighbouring points are compared by dragging along the congruence.
figures.visual_description: A single curve rising gently from left to right with points P and Q marked. At P a tangent arrow labelled X^a(P) and a longer arrow labelled 'Tensor' at P. At Q a tangent arrow X^a(Q), a solid arrow labelled 'Tensor' at Q, and a dashed arrow labelled 'Dragged-along tensor' at Q pointing in a different direction.
figures.what_it_teaches: The Lie derivative compares the field at Q with the version of the field at P carried by the flow; the gap between the dashed and solid arrows is what is differentiated.

redesign.idea: Lie dragging sandbox: a vector field Y is drawn over a flow X; the learner drags a point along an integral curve and sees Y(P) pushed forward by the flow (dashed) next to Y(Q) (solid), with the difference divided by du plotted and converging to [X,Y] as du shrinks.
redesign.interaction: Drag Q along the curve; slider for du; choose X and Y from presets including commuting pairs (difference stays zero) and rotation versus radial fields.

figures.label: Fig. 6.4
figures.caption_paraphrase: The point transformation moves P to Q within one coordinate chart.
figures.visual_description: A hatched, irregular sheet in perspective labelled x^a-coordinate chart. A curve crosses it with point P and a nearby point Q; a short arrow labelled X^a starts near P pointing toward Q.
figures.what_it_teaches: The active viewpoint: one chart, points moved by du X, rather than one point relabelled.

redesign.idea: Active versus passive toggle: the same small transformation shown once as a grid deforming under fixed points (passive) and once as points sliding over a fixed grid (active).
redesign.interaction: Switch mode; slider for du; watch component tables for a tensor at P update in both views.

figures.label: Fig. 6.5
figures.caption_paraphrase: The vector at Q parallel to X at P and the tensorial difference.
figures.visual_description: Point P at lower left with a vertical arrow X^a. At Q to the right, three arrows: a dashed arrow X^a + bar-delta X^a labelled 'Parallel' vector, a solid arrow X^a + delta X^a, and a short arrow joining their tips labelled delta X^a - bar-delta X^a.
figures.what_it_teaches: Covariant derivative as the difference between the actual field and the parallel-transported vector at the same point, which is the only tensorial difference.
concepts: parallel vector at a neighbouring point

redesign.idea: Connection dial: on a 2D plane with polar coordinates, show the field X at Q, the naive component-copied vector, and the genuinely parallel vector computed from Christoffel symbols; the learner sees component copying fail when coordinates curve.
redesign.interaction: Drag P and Q; switch between Cartesian and polar components; slider interpolating Gamma between zero and the polar Christoffel values to see which choice produces a coordinate-independent difference.

figures.label: Fig. 6.6
figures.caption_paraphrase: Two affine geodesics through P with prescribed directions.
figures.visual_description: Two smooth curves crossing at a point P; at P arrows indicate the two initial directions, one curve continuing up-right and one to the right.
figures.what_it_teaches: Each direction at a point determines a unique geodesic (ODE uniqueness).
concepts: local existence and uniqueness of geodesics

redesign.idea: Geodesic spray: on a sphere or saddle surface, the learner rotates an initial direction at P and sees the unique geodesic launched in that direction, with a fan of many directions shown at once.
redesign.interaction: Rotate direction handle; toggle full spray; change surface.

figures.label: Fig. 6.7
figures.caption_paraphrase: Two geodesics leaving P meet again at Q.
figures.visual_description: A lens shape: two curves both starting at a dot P at the bottom and bowing apart before meeting again at a dot Q at the top.
figures.what_it_teaches: Uniqueness of the geodesic between two points is only local; geodesics can focus.

redesign.idea: Refocusing on a sphere: meridians from the north pole meet at the south pole; a slider varies curvature so the refocusing point moves to infinity as the surface flattens.
redesign.interaction: Curvature slider; spread-angle slider; highlight the first conjugate point.

figures.label: Fig. 6.8
figures.caption_paraphrase: Parallel transport along two different curves gives different vectors.
figures.visual_description: A wavy ribbon-like surface in perspective. Two curves C1 (lower, solid) and C2 (upper) run from P on the left to Q on the right. Along C1 upright solid arrows are drawn; along C2 dashed arrows; at Q the arrows arriving by the two routes point in visibly different directions.
figures.what_it_teaches: Path dependence of parallel transport in a general affine manifold, the geometric content of non-zero curvature.

redesign.idea: Two-path transport on a sphere: the learner draws two paths from P to Q and watches a vector transported along each; the angle between arrivals is displayed and compared with the enclosed area times curvature.
redesign.interaction: Draw or drag path waypoints; toggle a flat plane or cylinder (angle zero) versus sphere or saddle; readout of angle mismatch.

figures.label: Fig. 6.9
figures.caption_paraphrase: Transport of X around an infinitesimal parallelogram.
figures.visual_description: A curvilinear quadrilateral with corners labelled x^a (left), x^a + delta x^a (top), x^a + delta x^a + Delta x^a (right) and x^a + Delta x^a (bottom). Arrows run along both routes from the left corner to the right corner; a small arrow X^a stands at the left corner.
figures.what_it_teaches: Set-up for the second-order computation showing the two routes differ by a Riemann term times the loop area element.
concepts: parallel transport around an infinitesimal loop

redesign.idea: Loop shrinker: on a curved surface a coordinate parallelogram with adjustable sides; the transported-vector mismatch divided by the area is plotted as the loop shrinks, converging to the curvature component.
redesign.interaction: Sliders for delta x and Delta x; readout of mismatch, area and their ratio; swap route order to show the sign flip.

figures.label: Fig. 6.10
figures.caption_paraphrase: Deforming curve C1 into C2 by infinitesimal steps.
figures.visual_description: A lens of curves from P on the left to Q on the right: the top curve labelled C1 and bottom curve labelled C2, with several intermediate curves between them, each differing slightly from its neighbours.
figures.what_it_teaches: Finite path independence follows from zero change around each thin loop between neighbouring curves, provided the region has no holes.

redesign.idea: Homotopy animation with a hole option: curves sweep from C1 to C2; with a puncture (e.g. cone tip) the sweep is blocked and transport around the hole can still rotate vectors despite zero local curvature.
redesign.interaction: Play sweep; toggle an obstacle; show accumulated rotation.

figures.label: Fig. 6.11
figures.caption_paraphrase: A manifold carries two families of geodesics, affine and metric.
figures.visual_description: A blob labelled Manifold M filled with two families of fine parallel lines crossing each other in a diagonal cross-hatch; labels with leader lines mark one family 'Affine geodesics' and the other 'Metric geodesics'.
figures.what_it_teaches: Straightest and shortest curves are defined by independent structures and need not coincide unless the connection is the metric one.

redesign.idea: Two straight-line notions on one surface: from a point, trace geodesics of an arbitrary user-tweaked connection and of the metric; add a torsion-free perturbation of Gamma away from Christoffel symbols and watch the families split, then snap back when the perturbation is set to zero.
redesign.interaction: Slider for the connection perturbation; shooting direction handle; overlay of the shortest path found numerically between two chosen points.

worked_examples.problem: Decide whether the partial derivatives of a vector field's components form a (1,1) tensor.
worked_examples.method: Differentiate the contravariant transformation law with respect to the new coordinates, using the chain rule to convert to old-coordinate derivatives and the product rule on the Jacobian factor.
worked_examples.key_insight: The extra term carries second derivatives of the coordinate change, which vanish only for linear transformations; the root cause is comparing components at different points.
worked_examples.result: Equation (6.1): tensor term plus inhomogeneous term, so d_b X^a is not a tensor.
concepts: non-tensorial character of the partial derivative
comparison of tensors at different points

worked_examples.problem: Derive the Lie derivative of a rank-2 contravariant tensor field along X.
