worked_examples.method: Apply the infinitesimal point map (6.3), expand its Jacobian (6.4), push T^ab forward with the tensor law to first order (6.5), Taylor expand the field at the new point (6.6), subtract and take the limit (6.7).
worked_examples.key_insight: Using the flow to carry the tensor removes the two-point problem without any connection; each upper index produces a -T d X correction from the Jacobian.
worked_examples.result: L_X T^ab = X^c d_c T^ab - T^ac d_c X^b - T^cb d_c X^a (6.8).

worked_examples.problem: Find how Gamma must transform if nabla_c X^a = d_c X^a + Gamma^a_bc X^b is to be a tensor, and extend the derivative to covectors and general tensors.
worked_examples.method: Demand the (1,1) law for nabla_c X^a, use (6.1) for the partial derivative and isolate Gamma' (Exercise 6.3); then impose nabla phi = d phi and the Leibniz rule on X_a Y^a (Exercise 6.5).
worked_examples.key_insight: The connection's inhomogeneous term is built to cancel exactly the inhomogeneous term of the partial derivative; Leibniz then fixes the sign for lower indices.

worked_examples.problem: Show that the affine geodesic property is independent of parametrization and that an affine parameter always exists.
worked_examples.method: Change parameter u -> u-tilde, express first and second derivatives by the chain rule, substitute into the geodesic equation, and read off the new coefficient lambda-tilde (6.35).
worked_examples.key_insight: Reparametrization only adds a term along the tangent, so it can be tuned to cancel lambda; the residual freedom is affine.
worked_examples.result: (6.36); choosing lambda-tilde = 0 gives (6.37) with s fixed up to alpha s + beta.

worked_examples.problem: Compute the commutator of two covariant derivatives acting on a vector.
worked_examples.method: Treat nabla_c X^a as a (1,1) tensor, apply (6.27) for the second derivative in both orders, subtract, and assume mixed partials of X commute.
worked_examples.key_insight: All terms with first derivatives of X cancel, leaving a piece linear in X (curvature) and a piece proportional to the torsion.
worked_examples.result: (6.39)-(6.41), defining R^a_bcd and proving it is a tensor.

worked_examples.problem: Construct coordinates at a point P in which a symmetric connection vanishes.
worked_examples.method: Put P at the origin, apply a quadratic change x' = x + (1/2) Q x x with constant symmetric Q, note the Jacobian is the identity at P, and substitute into (6.23).
worked_examples.key_insight: Only the symmetric part of Gamma can be cancelled by second derivatives of a coordinate change, and only at a point.
worked_examples.result: Gamma'(P) = Gamma(P) - Q, zero for Q = Gamma(P) (6.43).
concepts: inhomogeneous transformation law of the connection

worked_examples.problem: Prove that an integrable connection has vanishing Riemann tensor.
worked_examples.method: Integrability yields a covariantly constant field from any initial vector; its PDE (6.44) requires commuting mixed partials (6.45); rewrite the commutator identity to see this means R^a_bcd X^b = 0 for arbitrary X.
worked_examples.key_insight: Curvature is exactly the obstruction to solving nabla X = 0 for a full set of initial data.

worked_examples.problem: Show that transport around an infinitesimal loop changes a vector by a Riemann term, and hence R = 0 implies integrability.
worked_examples.method: Parallel displace X along delta x then Delta x, Taylor expanding Gamma at the intermediate point to second order; repeat in the opposite order; subtract, relabel dummy indices and compare with (6.40); extend to finite paths by deformation through thin loops (Fig. 6.10).
worked_examples.key_insight: The antisymmetric combination of second-order terms is precisely R^a_bdc; simple connectedness lets local path independence become global.
worked_examples.result: Delta X^a = -R^a_bcd X^b delta x^c Delta x^d.
concepts: parallel transport around an infinitesimal loop

worked_examples.problem: Prove that a symmetric integrable connection admits coordinates in which it vanishes everywhere.
worked_examples.method: Parallel propagate n independent vectors to get a frame, invert it to a dual frame, express Gamma through the frame (6.47)-(6.48), use symmetry to show each dual covector is curl-free and thus a gradient df^i, adopt f^i as coordinates and verify Gamma' = 0 via (6.23).
worked_examples.key_insight: Integrability gives a parallel frame; symmetry (no torsion) makes the frame holonomic, i.e. a coordinate basis.
worked_examples.result: Sufficiency half of Lemma 2, hence affine flat iff R = 0.

worked_examples.problem: Find the connection for which affine geodesics and metric geodesics coincide, and check its properties.
worked_examples.method: Compare the affinely parametrized equation (6.37) with the interval-parametrized metric equation (6.67) and identify Gamma with the Christoffel symbols; verify symmetry, connection law (Exercise 6.17), metric compatibility (Exercise 6.20) and uniqueness (Exercise 6.21, by cyclically permuting (6.77) and adding).
worked_examples.key_insight: One structure (the metric) can fix the other (the connection), making 'never turning' and 'extremal length' the same notion.
concepts: fundamental theorem for the metric connection

worked_examples.problem: Prove a metric is flat iff its Riemann tensor vanishes.
worked_examples.method: Necessity: constant +-1 metric gives zero Christoffel symbols everywhere, hence zero R. Sufficiency: R = 0 gives coordinates with Gamma = 0 everywhere (§6.7); then (6.77) forces d_c g_ab = 0, and a constant symmetric matrix can be diagonalized to +-1 by a linear change.
worked_examples.key_insight: Metric compatibility ties the constancy of g to the vanishing of Gamma, so affine and metric flatness coincide.
concepts: derivative of the metric in terms of the connection

worked_examples.problem: Count curvature components in dimensions 1 to 4 and split the four-dimensional count.
worked_examples.method: Evaluate n^2(n^2-1)/12 and compare with the number of components of the symmetric Ricci tensor, n(n+1)/2.
worked_examples.key_insight: In 2D curvature is one scalar, in 3D Ricci determines everything, and in 4D half the 20 components are invisible to Ricci and form the Weyl tensor.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Integral curves of a vector field are like field lines of an electric field or streamlines of a fluid flow.
analogies_and_intuitions.target_concept: integral curves of a vector field
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Invoked to make the ODE construction of a congruence from a vector field feel familiar.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Field lines in electromagnetism are usually drawn without a parameter; here the parametrization u matters because the Lie derivative uses the flow distance du.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Overlay a fluid tracer animation on the vector field so the flow parameter becomes elapsed time.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: In coordinates adapted to X, Lie differentiation is just ordinary partial differentiation along x^1.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Offered after (6.8) to demystify the formula: the correction terms are artefacts of using coordinates not aligned with the flow.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Adapted coordinates exist only where X is non-zero and only locally; they cannot be used for two non-commuting fields at once.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Morph a Cartesian grid into flow-adapted coordinates and show the Lie derivative formula's correction terms disappearing.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Two meanings of a straight line in Euclidean space: a line that never changes direction and the shortest route between two points.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Motivates why a manifold with both a connection and a metric has two geodesic families and why identifying them singles out the metric connection.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: In Lorentzian geometry timelike geodesics locally maximize rather than minimize interval, and null geodesics have zero length, so 'shortest' must be read as 'stationary'.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Side-by-side ant experiments: one ant walks without turning, the other finds the shortest string between pins; on a sphere with the Levi-Civita connection they agree, with a twisted connection they do not.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: A derivative of something that is zero everywhere must be zero, because the difference quotient subtracts zeros.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Parenthetical reassurance in the necessity proof that vanishing Gamma everywhere implies vanishing derivatives of Gamma, contrasted implicitly with geodesic coordinates where Gamma vanishes only at a point.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Only valid for vanishing on an open set, not at a single point.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: The null cone of a Lorentzian metric in each tangent space is the same structure met in special relativity.
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Transfers spacetime-diagram intuition for timelike, spacelike and null vectors to a general curved metric, pointwise.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: In curved spacetime cones tilt and change from point to point; there is no global Minkowski diagram.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Field of little light cones over a 2D spacetime chart that tilt as the learner edits metric functions.

analogies_and_intuitions.analogy: Deforming one path into another through a stack of neighbouring paths, each differing by a thin loop (Fig. 6.10).
analogies_and_intuitions.how_used: Turns the infinitesimal-loop result into path independence for finite paths.
analogies_and_intuitions.limits: Fails if the region has holes; the book mentions simple connectedness but gives no example of what goes wrong.
analogies_and_intuitions.app_idea: Cone surface with its tip removed: flat everywhere, yet vectors carried around the tip rotate, showing why the no-holes assumption is needed.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The partial derivative of a tensor's components is itself a tensor.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Under non-linear coordinate changes an extra second-derivative term appears (6.1); only the covariant or Lie derivative is tensorial.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: In Cartesian coordinates of flat space and in special relativity with Lorentz transformations the Jacobian is constant, so partials do behave like tensors.
concepts: non-tensorial character of the partial derivative

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The connection coefficients Gamma^a_bc form a tensor.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They transform inhomogeneously (6.23); they can be made zero at a point by a coordinate change, which no non-zero tensor allows. Differences of connections and the torsion are tensors, sums are not.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: They carry three indices in tensor positions and appear in tensor equations.
concepts: inhomogeneous transformation law of the connection

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: If the connection vanishes at a point in geodesic coordinates, spacetime is flat there, or its derivatives vanish too.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Geodesic coordinates remove Gamma only at P; its first derivatives, and hence the Riemann tensor, generally survive. Removing Gamma on a whole neighbourhood is possible only when R = 0.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Zero Christoffel symbols is the usual computational signature of flat Cartesian coordinates.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: A geodesic is always the shortest path between two points.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Metric geodesics make the interval stationary: a maximum, minimum or saddle; timelike geodesics in a Lorentzian metric locally maximize interval, null geodesics have zero interval.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Euclidean intuition and the common slogan 'shortest distance'.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Affine parameter values measure the same length on any two geodesics.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Each geodesic's affine parameter is fixed only up to s -> alpha s + beta, so affine lengths compare segments on one geodesic only; comparing different geodesics needs a metric.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The word 'length' suggests a universal ruler.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Geodesics and parallel transport are metric notions.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Affine geodesics and parallel transport need only a connection; the metric enters only in §6.8, and the Lie derivative needs neither.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Most GR courses introduce the metric first and derive Gamma from it.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The eigenvalues of the metric matrix are geometric invariants.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Eigenvalues change with coordinates; only the count of positive and negative ones (the signature) is invariant.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Eigenvalues of a linear operator are invariant, but g_ab is a bilinear form, which transforms by congruence rather than similarity.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Once indices can be raised and lowered, their horizontal order does not matter.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: X_a^b and X^b_a are generally different; order of slots must be preserved when moving indices.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Symmetric tensors like g_ab and R_ab hide the issue.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Covariant derivatives commute like partial derivatives.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Their commutator is governed by the Riemann tensor (and torsion); commuting holds for all tensors only when R = 0 and the connection is symmetric.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Mixed partial derivatives commute and nabla looks like a partial derivative plus a correction.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: The Weyl tensor is conformally invariant in any index position.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Only C^a_bcd with one index up is unchanged by g -> Omega^2 g; lowering or raising uses the rescaled metric and introduces powers of Omega.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Raising and lowering is usually treated as mere notation.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Conformally related metrics describe the same geometry.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: They share angles, length ratios, null geodesics and the Weyl tensor, but not lengths, timelike geodesics, the connection or the Riemann tensor.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: Light cones, and thus causal structure, look identical.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: All authors' Riemann and Ricci tensors agree in sign.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: Sign conventions for Riemann, Ricci and the signature vary; formulas must be translated between books.

misconceptions_addressed.misconception: Vanishing Riemann tensor alone guarantees affine flatness for any connection.
misconceptions_addressed.correction: The book's theorem assumes a symmetric connection; with torsion, a connection can have zero curvature yet no coordinates make Gamma vanish, as Lemma 2 requires symmetry.
misconceptions_addressed.why_tempting: The final theorem box omits the standing symmetry assumption.

thought_experiments.name: Comparing arrows at two points by dragging along a flow
thought_experiments.setup: A tensor at P is carried along the integral curve of X to Q using the flow, and set beside the tensor field's actual value at Q (Fig. 6.3).
thought_experiments.lesson: Any derivative needs a rule for moving tensors between points; the flow supplies one without metric or connection, and the mismatch rate is the Lie derivative.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Drag a small arrow along streamlines of a rotating flow and compare with a painted field at the destination.

thought_experiments.name: Transport along two routes
thought_experiments.setup: A vector at P is parallel transported to Q along two different curves C1 and C2 in a general affine manifold (Fig. 6.8).
thought_experiments.lesson: The results differ unless the connection is integrable; everyday parallelism is a special property of flat spaces.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Transport a gyroscope-like arrow along two chosen paths on a globe and measure the angle between arrivals.

thought_experiments.name: Tiny parallelogram circuit
thought_experiments.setup: A vector is carried around an infinitesimal coordinate parallelogram with sides delta x and Delta x, comparing the two halves of the circuit (Fig. 6.9).
thought_experiments.lesson: The mismatch is second order, proportional to the enclosed coordinate area element and to the Riemann tensor.
concepts: parallel transport around an infinitesimal loop
thought_experiments.app_idea: Shrink a loop on a sphere and plot mismatch against area to extract curvature.

thought_experiments.name: Geodesics that meet again
thought_experiments.setup: Two affine geodesics leave P in different directions and are followed far enough that they intersect at Q (Fig. 6.7).
thought_experiments.lesson: Local uniqueness of the geodesic joining two points does not extend globally.
thought_experiments.app_idea: Great circles from a pole meeting at the antipode, with a curvature slider.

historical_notes.event: The curvature tensor is named the Riemann-Christoffel tensor and the metric-derived connection symbols the Christoffel symbols of the first and second kind.
historical_notes.significance: The only historical traces in this chapter are eponyms; the book gives no dates or narrative, and the Bianchi, Ricci, Weyl, Lie and Einstein names likewise appear only as labels.

applications_and_observations.details: The metric of relativity has one positive and three negative eigenvalues, signature -2, carrying the special-relativistic null cone into each tangent space. Exercise 6.22 checks signature, non-singularity and flatness of the Minkowski line element.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: signature -2 = 1 - 3; the +2 convention flips all signs

applications_and_observations.details: Riemann components drop from n^4 to n^2(n^2-1)/12. In spacetime 20 remain, of which 10 are fixed by the Ricci tensor and 10 are Weyl. Own framing (not in this chapter): the field equations will tie the Ricci part to matter locally, leaving the Weyl part for tidal fields and gravitational waves in vacuum.
applications_and_observations.key_numbers: n=2: 1; n=3: 6; n=4: 20 = 10 + 10; unconstrained n^4 = 256 in 4D

applications_and_observations.topic: Size of the connection and metric (own estimate)
applications_and_observations.details: A general connection in n dimensions has n^3 components; a symmetric one n^2(n+1)/2; the metric has n(n+1)/2. In 4D these are 64, 40 and 10, which motivates exploiting symmetry (e.g. Exercise 6.32) when computing curvature by hand. These counts are our own arithmetic, not stated in the text beyond n^3.

applications_and_observations.topic: Curvature of the general spherically symmetric metric
applications_and_observations.details: Exercise 6.32 asks for g_ab, Christoffel symbols, Riemann, Ricci, Ricci scalar and mixed Einstein tensor for ds^2 = e^nu dt^2 - e^lambda dr^2 - r^2(dtheta^2 + sin^2 theta dphi^2) with nu, lambda functions of t and r, flagged as needed later for the Schwarzschild solution (Chapter 15, equation (15.37)).

notation_and_conventions.notes: The book notes the opposite (+2) convention used elsewhere.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Written d_b X^a, dX^a/dx^b or X^a_{,b}; the book mixes the first three. Also called the ordinary derivative.
notation_and_conventions.notes: X^a_{|b} is listed as another notation in the literature.

notation_and_conventions.convention: Written nabla_c X^a or X^a_{;c} (also X^a_{||c} in the literature); derivative index is the last lower index on Gamma.
An equals sign with an asterisk marks an equation valid only in a particular coordinate system (e.g. adapted or geodesic coordinates).
Roman L with subscript X: L_X T.
D/Du along a curve with parameter u; nabla_X for contraction with X.
Triple bar marks identities holding for all tensors/metrics, e.g. nabla_c g_ab identically 0, Bianchi identities.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Continues the identity-versus-equation distinction from Chapter 5.

notation_and_conventions.convention: First kind {ab,c}; second kind as a brace with a above bc. After §6.10 the metric connection is written Gamma^a_bc.
R^a_bcd = d_c Gamma^a_bd - d_d Gamma^a_bc + Gamma^e_bd Gamma^a_ec - Gamma^e_bc Gamma^a_ed, so [nabla_c, nabla_d] X^a = R^a_bcd X^b.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Same Riemann and Ricci index conventions as Misner-Thorne-Wheeler, though MTW use signature +2.

notation_and_conventions.convention: R_ab = R^c_acb, contracting first and third indices.
Bold i labels members of a set of n vector fields X_i^a and is summed over like a tensor index but is not a coordinate index.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Bold type is lost in the text export of §6.7.

notation_and_conventions.convention: The same letter denotes a tensor with any index positions, e.g. T_ab, T_a^b, T^a_b, T^ab.
notation_and_conventions.notes: Horizontal index order must be kept.

notation_and_conventions.convention: ds^2 means (ds)^2; ds is called distance in Riemannian and interval in relativistic contexts; d sigma is used for spacelike separations.
Square brackets on indices anti-symmetrize with a normalizing factor, as in nabla_[c nabla_d] X^a = (1/2) R^a_bcd X^b.

margin_notes.summary: Before the Lie derivative argument the authors warn that it is intricate, and point out that its key outputs, the general formula and the list of properties, come at the end of the section.
The minus sign in the parallel displacement ansatz is chosen to match the standard convention for Gamma.
Reader is reminded twice that the differentiation index sits last on Gamma and that the covector term carries a minus sign.
From §6.3 on, connections are assumed symmetric unless stated otherwise.
Even a non-symmetric connection would enter the geodesic equation only through its symmetric part.
Unanswered 'why?' prompts ask why the metric has no zero eigenvalues and why the signature is coordinate independent.
The derivation of the metric geodesic equations via the calculus of variations is postponed to the next chapter.
Equation (6.77) expressing metric derivatives through the connection is flagged as useful later.
Some authors use the opposite sign for the Riemann or Ricci tensor.
Exercise 6.32 is flagged as a long calculation that will be needed later, citing the spherically symmetric line element of Chapter 15.

Further reading repeats the Chapter 5 list: Choquet-Bruhat et al., Hughston and Tod, Landau and Lifshitz, MTW, O'Neill, Penrose (1968), Penrose and Rindler, Schutz (1980, 1985), Synge and Schild. The suspect short page 128 contains only the tail of this list.

notable.summary: Derive the inhomogeneous transformation law of the connection by demanding that the covariant derivative be a (1,1) tensor, then convert it to the alternative form by differentiating the Jacobian-inverse identity.
notable.why_notable: Completes the core definitional step of §6.3 that the text leaves as an exercise.

notable.summary: Show that the commutator of nabla_X and nabla_Y acting on Z, corrected by nabla along the Lie bracket, equals the Riemann tensor contracted with Z, X and Y.
notable.why_notable: Gives the index-free definition of curvature used in modern texts and links §6.2 to §6.5.

notable.summary: Compute the metric connection of flat 3-space in cylindrical polar coordinates and write out the geodesic equations.
notable.why_notable: The only concrete Christoffel-symbol computation for a familiar space; shows non-zero Gamma in flat space.

notable.summary: For a three-dimensional line element with coordinates x, y, z, show that the null geodesics are straight lines whose direction numbers satisfy a quadratic null condition.
notable.why_notable: The printed line element is positive definite (all plus signs), which has no null geodesics; the condition l^2 + m^2 - n^2 = 0 requires ds^2 = dx^2 + dy^2 - dz^2. A likely printed sign error.

notable.summary: Show that any symmetric connection with covariantly constant metric must be the metric connection, by writing compatibility for three index orderings and combining.
notable.why_notable: Proves the uniqueness half of the fundamental theorem; the permutation trick recurs throughout GR.

notable.summary: Identify an unfamiliar-looking line element as flat 3-space in spherical polars and decide whether it is flat.
notable.why_notable: Tests the distinction between non-constant metric components and genuine curvature.

notable.summary: Derive how the metric connection and Riemann tensor change under a conformal rescaling written through derivatives of ln Omega, and deduce invariance of the Weyl tensor.
notable.why_notable: Supplies the proof behind (6.92). The printed part (iii) expression contains index inconsistencies (e.g. a free index appearing twice in one term), so learners should derive it and check with computer algebra rather than match the print.

notable.summary: For the general time-dependent spherically symmetric line element with two arbitrary functions, compute the metric inverse, Christoffel symbols, Riemann, Ricci, Ricci scalar and mixed Einstein tensor.
notable.why_notable: Explicitly needed for the Schwarzschild derivation in Chapter 15 and for Birkhoff-type arguments; ideal target for a guided computer-algebra demo.

difficulty.notes: Dense index calculus with many derivations delegated to exercises and no worked numerical example (no sphere, no polar coordinates) inside the text. The Lie derivative via active point transformations and the lemma proofs of §6.7 are the hardest parts; §6.8-6.12 are standard but terse. Physics motivation is entirely absent, so learners without a reason to care about curvature may lose the thread.

cross_references.reason: Tensor transformation laws (5.18) and (5.30) are differentiated in (6.1) and reused to drag tensors in (6.5).
Anti-symmetrization bracket (5.33) used to write the commutator (6.41).
Vector fields as operators and the Lie bracket, identified with L_X Y in (6.15); tangent space T_P M hosts the null cone.
Invariance of the Kronecker delta is recalled for Exercise 6.1.
Null cone and timelike/spacelike/null classification from special relativity carried into each tangent space.
Promised geometric characterization of vanishing Riemann tensor, announced in §6.5.
Variational derivation of the metric geodesic equations quoted in §6.9, and the Lagrangian shortcut for Christoffel symbols.
Active transformations, Lie derivative of the metric and Killing vectors build on §6.2.
The metric-determinant section combines (6.77) with the derivative of g to get the contracted connection and covariant derivatives of densities.

Teaching link, not a citation found in ch09: geodesic coordinates, where Gamma vanishes at a point, are the mathematical counterpart of local freely falling frames, and affine geodesics supply the free-fall worldlines.
Einstein tensor and contracted Bianchi identities (6.86)-(6.87) become the left side of the field equations and guarantee consistency with conservation.
Geodesic coordinates, (6.40) and metric compatibility used to derive the Palatini identity.
Exercise 6.32 supplies the curvature of the spherically symmetric metric (15.37); Exercise 6.28 motivates isotropic coordinates.
Conformal flatness of 2D metrics (Exercise 6.31) and shared null geodesics (Exercise 6.29) justify Penrose diagrams.
In vacuum Riemann equals Weyl by (6.88). The Weyl tensor's symmetries and trace-freeness feed the Petrov classification and the peeling theorem.
Classical component-based source whose style (parallel displacement ansatz, geodesic coordinates) the chapter follows.

teaching_gems.gem: Diagnose once, reuse thrice: every derivative fails because it subtracts objects at different points, and each new structure (flow, connection, metric) is just a rule for bringing them together.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Gives learners a single organizing question for three constructions that otherwise look unrelated.
teaching_gems.app_idea: A 'how do I compare these arrows?' hub page with three tabs (drag by flow, transport by connection, transport by metric connection), each showing the same two-point comparison with a different rule.

teaching_gems.gem: Lie derivative as dragging with the flow, then subtracting at one point; in flow-adapted coordinates it is just d/dx^1.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Separates the geometric idea from the index formula and explains the correction terms as coordinate artefacts.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Lie dragging sandbox with a du slider showing the difference quotient converging to the bracket [X,Y].

teaching_gems.gem: Define the connection through a triangle of arrows at Q: actual field, parallel copy, and their tensorial difference (Fig. 6.5).
teaching_gems.why_effective: Makes nabla X = d X + Gamma X read as 'change minus the change you would have had anyway', and explains the minus sign.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Polar-coordinate plane where the learner sees component-copying fail and Christoffel-corrected transport succeed.

teaching_gems.gem: Two notions of straight line (never turning, extremal length) that coincide exactly for the metric connection.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Motivates the Christoffel formula as the answer to a geometric question rather than a memorized expression.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Perturb a connection away from Levi-Civita and watch straightest and shortest paths from one point separate.

teaching_gems.gem: Curvature as the second-order failure of a vector to return unchanged around a tiny parallelogram, computed explicitly by Taylor expansion.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Connects the algebraic commutator definition to a measurable holonomy with a clear area scaling.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Loop shrinker on a sphere plotting angle mismatch against area, recovering Gaussian curvature as the slope.

teaching_gems.gem: Geodesic coordinates: a quadratic coordinate tweak kills Gamma at one point but cannot touch its derivatives.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Short, concrete construction that pinpoints why curvature is coordinate-invariant and prefigures local inertial frames.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Coordinate grid warping around P in which the Christoffel readout at P goes to zero while the Riemann readout stays unchanged.

teaching_gems.gem: Flatness from a parallel frame: path independence gives a frame, torsion-freeness makes its dual covectors gradients, and those gradients are Cartesian coordinates.
teaching_gems.why_effective: Constructive proof showing exactly what role integrability and symmetry each play.
teaching_gems.app_idea: On a plane with curvilinear coordinates, transport a frame everywhere, then integrate the dual covectors to reconstruct Cartesian grid lines.

teaching_gems.gem: Counting components in n = 1..4 to motivate the Weyl tensor as the curvature Ricci cannot see.
teaching_gems.why_effective: A quick arithmetic table explains why 4D is the first dimension with independent 'free' curvature.
teaching_gems.app_idea: Dimension slider with a bar split into Ricci and Weyl components.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: No concrete example in the text: connection, parallel transport, geodesics and curvature are never computed for a sphere, a plane in polar coordinates or any explicit metric (only in exercises).
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners can manipulate indices without ever seeing a non-zero Christoffel symbol in flat space or a non-zero curvature.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Pair §6.3-6.5 with polar coordinates on the plane and the 2-sphere, computing Gamma, a geodesic and R^theta_phi theta phi explicitly.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed slip in the loop argument: the second route is described as going via x + delta x, but it goes via x + Delta x.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Confuses which two routes are being compared and the sign of the result.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: State clearly: route A through x + delta x, route B through x + Delta x, and ask learners to check the relabelling of dummy indices.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed slip in geodesic coordinates: the Jacobian of the quadratic transformation is printed with x^d where x^b is needed.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A repeated index appearing three times breaks the summation convention and may stall a careful reader.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Write d x'^a / d x^d = delta^a_d + Q^a_bd x^b.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Printed slips in the exercises, each checked on the rendered pages. Exercise 6.19 (pdf p.125) gives a positive definite line element but asks for null geodesics with l^2 + m^2 - n^2 = 0. Exercise 6.7(i) (pdf p.124) has nu where mu is meant. Exercise 6.30(iii) (pdf p.126) repeats a free index within a single term.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may waste time or doubt correct work.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Use ds^2 = dx^2 + dy^2 - dz^2 in 6.19 and verify 6.30(iii) with computer algebra.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The final flatness theorem box omits the standing assumption that the connection is symmetric, and the global statement also needs simple connectedness.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Readers may believe R = 0 alone implies flatness for any connection on any manifold.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Restate: for a torsion-free connection on a simply connected region, flat iff R = 0; show a cone or a teleparallel connection as counterexamples.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The Weyl conformal flatness theorem is stated without its dimension restriction (n >= 4); in 3D the Weyl tensor vanishes identically though not every 3-metric is conformally flat (the Cotton tensor decides). The 2D result is local.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Overgeneralization to three dimensions and to global statements.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Add the n >= 4 caveat and mention the Cotton tensor in a side note.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Metric geodesics are defined as stationary-interval curves using a square-root Lagrangian, but null curves have zero interval, so the variational definition does not apply to them; the book simply asserts the null geodesic equation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Unclear why null geodesics satisfy the same equation or what 'affine parameter' means for them before Chapter 7.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Preview the quadratic Lagrangian g(dx/du, dx/du) of Chapter 7, or define null geodesics as null affine geodesics of the metric connection after §6.10.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Christoffel symbols appear in §6.9 before being identified with the connection in §6.10, with two notations for the same object.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Learners may think Christoffel symbols and Gamma are unrelated objects.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Announce early that the brace symbols will turn out to be the connection coefficients of the metric.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The Lie derivative derivation uses active transformations that the text itself calls intricate, with no picture of the flow map acting on a whole field and no example calculation.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Sign errors (dragging forward versus pulling back) and confusion over why the formula differs from the covariant derivative.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Compute L_X Y for X a rotation field and Y a constant field in the plane, and animate the dragging.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: Several 'why?' prompts on signature and many '(exercise)' steps are left without hints in the text, including the tensor character of g^ab and of R.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Self-learners can miss key logical steps such as Sylvester's law of inertia.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Provide short tutor-side answers: congruence transformations preserve inertia; quotient theorem for R; primed version of (6.57) for g^ab.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: No physical interpretation of Riemann, Ricci or Einstein tensors (e.g. tidal forces, geodesic deviation, volume change) is offered here.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: Curvature feels purely formal until later chapters.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Foreshadow geodesic deviation and tidal acceleration when introducing R, and note that G_ab will equal a source term.

gaps_and_pitfalls.issue: The second closing theorem of §6.13 is stated only for two-dimensional Riemannian metrics. The Lorentzian version is left to Exercise 6.31, yet ch18 cites 'the second theorem in §6.13' for a Lorentzian 2-space.
gaps_and_pitfalls.impact_on_learner: A learner may not see why a result stated for positive definite metrics justifies the double null coordinates behind Penrose diagrams.
gaps_and_pitfalls.suggestion: Treat Exercise 6.31, which builds null coordinates for a 2D Lorentzian metric, as the version actually needed later, and work it before ch18.

tutor_notes: Open with: 'In Cartesian coordinates the derivative of a vector field is obvious. What goes wrong in polar coordinates, even on a flat plane?' Let the learner discover that basis vectors change from point to point before showing (6.1).
Keep one organizing question in view: how do I compare a tensor at P with one at Q? Present Lie dragging, parallel transport and the metric connection as three answers.

Order of explanation: non-tensorial partial derivative -> Lie derivative idea (flow) with a planar example -> connection via Fig. 6.5 triangle -> covariant derivative formulas and sign rules -> parallel transport and geodesics -> commutator and Riemann -> geodesic coordinates -> loop holonomy and flatness -> metric -> metric connection -> identities -> Ricci, Einstein -> Weyl and conformal.
Check for understanding: ask why Gamma can vanish at a point but R cannot be made to vanish by coordinates; a good answer mentions the inhomogeneous law and tensor character.
Check sign rules with a quick drill: Lie derivative has minus per upper index with d X; covariant derivative has plus per upper index with Gamma. Ask the learner to write L_X and nabla_c for T^a_b.

When a learner asks why we need a connection if we have a metric, explain that the book separates them deliberately: affine geodesics and parallel transport need only Gamma; the metric then selects a unique torsion-free compatible Gamma.
Common question: 'Is a geodesic the shortest path?' Answer with stationary interval, the Lorentzian maximization of proper time, and zero length for null geodesics.
Common question: 'Why does the Lie derivative not need a connection?' Answer: the flow of X itself provides the identification of nearby points and tensors; show (6.29) to see Gamma cancels anyway.
Flag book-specific conventions early: signature -2, R^a_bcd with MTW-style indices, Ricci contraction on first and third index; warn when mixing with Schutz or Carroll (signature +2).
Point out the printed slips (via Delta x in §6.7, x^b in §6.6, Exercise 6.19 sign) if the learner is working from the book, to prevent loss of confidence.
For advanced learners, connect §6.7 to holonomy and teleparallel (torsionful, curvature-free) connections; for beginners, stay with the sphere and the plane.
Use Exercise 6.32 (spherically symmetric metric) as a capstone, ideally with a computer-algebra demo so the learner sees the pipeline metric -> Gamma -> Riemann -> Ricci -> Einstein.
